speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RESULT OF THE PLEBISCITE-QUESTION AS TO ACTION BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the house while I make a brief statement and put a question to the ministry. The people of Canada yesterday spoke emphatically. Now there is no stumbling block, real or imaginary, to total war. The hour has struck when every human and material resource must be mobilized for war service. Parliament now is free to act-there are no fetters upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or his government. Let us act, and act now. We can decide and decide now that nothing shall limit our effort and we can repeal now those limiting or restricting

features. I invite the Prime Minister to respond to the people's will for total war, waged by total effort. Let him rise to the occasion now, and he will strike a great blow for victory. Let us go forward to greater and ever greater effort, secure in the knowledge that the people of Canada are ready and prepared for the sacrifices which that will entail.
The right of way is clear. What does the government propose to do about it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

I hope my hon. friend
will be content to wait until the final returns of the plebiscite have been given to the house before he asks me to discuss any matters arising out of it. In due course the government will make known to the house what action it proposes to take in the light of the plebiscite vote of yesterday.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, April 23, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding 82,000,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1943, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Before the discussion becomes general I desire to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). The minister will recall that on March 24 last, on a question of privilege, referred to at page 1583-4 of Hansard of that date, I asked him certain questions relating to a report, No. 47, sent out by -the military intel-* ligence section of the Department of National Defence, entitled, "Summaiy of Military Intelligence for Military Districts." This was referred to in the debate on the United Kingdom financing resolution on the Friday previous, March 20, by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix), as reported at page 1494 of Hansard. I then asked the minister three questions.
1.	Has the attention of the minister been called to this portion of the -hon. member's speech?
2.	Will the minister advise the house how the hon. member came into possession of what I assume to be a confidential military intelligence release?
3.	What does the minister propose to do about the matter in the premises?
The minister replied categorically: First, that his attention had been called to the report of the speech; secondly, that he had not the faintest idea of how the report came into the hands of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency; and thirdly, that the -most rigorous investigation was being conducted to ascertain who was responsible for the hon. member receiving the copy and that appropriate action would be taken according to the circumstances.
I now desire to ask the minister what was the result of the most rigorous investigation to which he referred: how did the hon. member obtain the copy of the report; and what was the appropriate action taken in the circumstances?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have not made inquiries in the last few days. I have asked the vicechief of the general staff to look into the matter but he has not yet been able to ascertain how the hon. member got possession of the document or through whom. The investigation is still continuing and I assure the committee that from the point of view of the department as well as of the house it will not be discontinued until evei-y possibility is exhausted of ascertaining how it was that this particular document got into the hands of anyone outside the department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am satisfied so long as the matter has not been lost sight of.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The points which I desire to bring to the attention of the committee this afternoon are confined very largely to matters affecting the morale and general conditions of the men and women of our armed forces. I shall not have a great deal to say, but I wish to touch upon one or two matters which I think are of prime importance and which, I believe, have engaged the attention not only of those in the armed forces but also of the public at large.
The whole question with respect to parity of pay and allowances in connection with our armed forces is, I realize, a matter that must be dealt with in the light of common sense and sober judgment in times like these, but I would call the attention of the minister and of the government to one particular phase of the situation which was originally brought before the house by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) and which later on was touched upon by myself. It is something that is very close to my heart and which on numerous occasions outside this house I have dwelt upon. Whatever may have been in the government's mind with respect to the question of rates of pay and allowances for our armed forces, there is one matter which has been to a large extent overlooked, whatever the reason may be.
I do not know what reasons may properly be advanced against a general rise in pay for the armed forces and I have never been greatly convinced by some of the arguments which have been put forward on that score, but I suggest that the government might well do
War Appropriation

something now with regard, to an alternative method by which the same object may be attained. I refer to a plan of savings, or a savings rehabilitation fund, which I mentioned in the house before and which I urge again. I believe we could do a great deal towards improving the morale not only of our men in the armed forces but of the people at home by a system of this type. In my opinion, the idea of a nest-egg for the men in the armed forces when this war is over has a twofold object. It would be a twofold achievement at the present time. One thing that occurs to me right away is the fact that it would bring up the standard of returns to the armed forces of Canada to a point at least within measurable parity with the returns which other people on the home front may be receiving. In addition to enhancing morale, which would normally flow from such a change, it would wipe out at one fell swoop many of the rehabilitation problems which various departments of the government are attempting to deal with and which they will have to solve at the end of the war.
I think the nest-egg plan, of putting something in addition to his present pay aside every month while the soldier or airman or sailor serves, can be justified on every ground-in the first place, on the ground1 of morale and secondly, it would remove one of the great obstacles to rehabilitation when the war is over. With all deference to those who have spoken from the government benches during the last few weeks on the very laudable efforts that have been made with respect to rehabilitation of the men in our forces, I would say that these are all promises relating to things to be done after the men are discharged. But I should like to see the government take hold of this problem and make sure that the men of our armed forces know that day by day and month by month, in addition to the rates of pay and allowances they are receiving, the government is setting aside a substantial savings fund for their use when they return. I want to emphasize that idea and impress it upon the minister.
Further with respect to the question of higher pay for our armed forces, I do not want the idea to become general that every little while someone must get up and raise that question just for the purpose of hearing himself speak. The reason I am making this statement now is that I honestly and sincerely believe that the programme which has been outlined, of a nest-egg for our armed forces, is not only justified but is

long overdue so far as government policy is concerned. I should like to see the minister take this matter into consideration without further delay. If there is no good basis for it, the government should let us know; we should at least be given some explanation and some assurance that the matter will be considered carefully from every possible angle.
I know, as does the minister, that in the United States legislative changes relating to this subject are now under consideration in the congress. To what extent they will improve standards with respect to returns to men of the armed forces I am. not prepared to say, but at least the United States congress has seriously under consideration legislation to improve the position of men in the forces of that country.
Also I want to say to the minister-perhaps I should do this when the estimates of the minister of naval services are before the committee, but I want to brin-g it to the attention of the Minister of National Defence -that there does not appear to me to be any justification for the vast difference in pay and in dependents' allowances of the naval services and the other services of Canada. Without any reflection on any of the other branches of the forces I am sure the people of Canada are sufficiently proud of the achievements of the officers and men of the navy to rise up in a body and cheer any government that would place that service at least upon an equal footing with the other services.
I come now to the question of dependents' allowances. In a speech made to this house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) on November 14 last in relation to war allowances and provision for a board of trustees to look after dependents, the minister set out a plan which I think the country welcomed. But in the light of subsequent events that announcement fell short of being any real solution of the problem of increased allowances to the kin of the men on service. The trustee board deals largely with emergencies outside the normal course of life. The minister did not take into sufficient consideration the rising cost of living, which bears with great force upon the dependents of the men serving in our armed forces.
I took the trouble to make some investigation into the increase in the cost of living since the beginning of the war. At the beginning of the war a private in the army was entitled to dependents' allowance of $35 monthly outside of the provision made for

War Appropriation
children. I have no doubt that that allowance was based upon the cost of living as it existed at the outbreak of the war. But if it was a proper allowance in September, 1939- and I am sure the government must have given it every consideration; if they were convinced that $35 a month was a proper allowance for the wife of a private at that time, then surely the government must now take into consideration the rise in the cost of living since that time. Let me give a few figures which I have obtained from the bureau of statistics. In August 1939 the index figure was set at 100. By December 2, 1940, a year and three months later, the cost of living in Canada had increased 7-1 per cent. By August 1941 it had increased by 12-8 per cent, and on March 2 of this year the cost of living had risen, not 7 per cent, not 12 per cent, but 15 per cent over what it was when the war broke out. That gives us this very simple equation:	If $35 a month was a proper
figure at the outbreak of the war, now that the cost of living has increased 15 per cent I submit that the allowance for the wife of a man in the armed forces-I am speaking particularly of the army-should be $40.25 a month.
True, it may be said that the government has extended the field in which dependents' allowances may be paid; in other words have added an allowance for a third child and for a fourth. But that is merely a rectification of an obvious error at the beginning and can scarcely be regarded as an argument that the government has increased the rate of allowance so far as the wife is concerned. Order in council P.C. 8253 provided for a cost of living bonus of 25 cents a week for each 1 per cent increase in the official index figure over that of August 1939. If my figures are correct it would mean that the allowance paid to the wife of a private in the army, instead of $40.25, would be increased to $50 per month. I leave these figures with the minister, with the suggestion that this is not something to be bandied about this committee for the sake of argument, but something to which I hope the minister will give careful consideration, and which he might take up with the Minister of Finance. Many times it is argued here that something cannot be done because of the cost to the treasury. That is always an important consideration, but I do not think it is a consideration which should be the last word when we are dealing with the dependents of men who are risking their lives for all of us on the home and overseas fronts. I hope the minister will give this suggestion the comprehensive consideration which I feel it richly deserves.
I am going to offer another suggestion, also having to do with the morale and general welfare of our forces. I know this point has been brought before the house previously, and I raise it now only to emphasize the need for some change in this respect. Many good arguments may be advanced by the government and others against the general granting of free transportation to soldiers, airmen and sailors. Perhaps there are good reasons why that should not be done, but it seems to me the reason would have to be extremely good for the government to turn down the suggestion that in connection with furlough leaves and particularly embarkation leaves, free transportation should be made available to the armed forces. Since this war began the government have found ways and means of doing many things; surely ways and means can be found of seeing to it that the men of our armed forces are not required to scrimp and save out of their meagre pittance for months at a time in order to pay their transportation back home to their loved ones before they leave for overseas. I want to impress upon the minister the importance, in my view in any event, of making some change which will bring about free transportation for our soldiers on their furlough and embarkation leaves.
Let me say further that I am not so sure it is good for the morale of the soldier, or for the morale of any of us, that there should be any distinctions on the railways of this country. Some people are allowed to travel free, while others are not. If there is to be any distinction made; if any are to travel free, then let it be the men who are willing to lay down their lives for us. Surely that is not too much to ask, and I make this plea to the minister. I know that the question has been brought up time after time, but I do -want to make this one last appeal. I have spoken to many of these men. I know what they say and what they think, and, in view of that I am going to offer another suggestion, if there is still any doubt in the mind of the minister. This may not be quite orthodox, as far as military matters are concerned, but these are not the days of orthodox things. I suggest that the minister choose ten men from among the privates in the ranks of our army in Canada; have them form a select committee to meet with him, and get right to the root of this question. He could find out from them their views, and I think the views of the whole army, with respect to the matters I have mentioned, and particularly with respect to this question of free transportation on furlough and embarkation leave. I would not make this suggestion
War Appropriation

if it would affect in any way the discipline of the armed forces, if it had anything to do with questions of seniority or anything of the kind. This, however, is a matter entirely apart, having nothing whatever to do with the discipline or organization of the army. It seems to me that nothing would better show the democratic spirit of this great country than for the minister to select ten or more men from the ranks of our armed forces to advise him on this and similar matters. I hope the minister will give this suggestion his careful consideration.
There is one other question I should like to ask the minister, which he might answer in the course of his statement. This situation has been brought to my attention by men in the air force, but I must confess that I have not had it brought to my notice by men in the army. In connection with embarkation leave, we will take a man in camp in eastern Canada who has to travel perhaps thousands of miles in order to get home. I should like the minister to give the committee some explanation or some information as to whether or not the time required for that man to reach his home is added to his embarkation leave, or whether the time spent in travelling is included in the normal leave. I should like it very much if the minister could give us that information during the course of his remarks.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend referred first to the matter of deferred pay. I take it that he was really referring to an additional amount which would be deferred until after the war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Quite so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then there is no question that my hon. friend was advocating an increase in pay, and simply deferring the time of payment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am not apologizing for it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am not asking my hon. friend to apologize, but I want to be clear about the matter, because as my hon. friend knows there is provision now for deferred pay. My hon. friend was rather protesting that he was not arguing for an increase in pay, but that was exactly what his suggestion amounted to. I am not arguing against it at the moment-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I meant increased cash pay.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: For my own information would the minister say what the position is with regard to deferred pay?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The provision with regard to deferred pay applies only to those who are overseas. If no assignment of pay has been made, then fifty per cent of the pay is deferred. If less than fifty per cent has been assigned the difference between the amount which has been assigned and 50 per cent of the pay is deferred. Those are the two points. That deferred pay is held at 3 per cent until the man is discharged or appointed to a commission. There are certain cases in which the deferred pay may be drawn upon. I know that at least every two or three days I sign authorizations for men to draw against their deferred pay. I believe marriage is one reason; or if there is illness on the part of his relatives, and I think there are some educational matters-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does that apply to both officers and men?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: -for which he may obtain authority to draw against his deferred pay.

speechtext:
Is there
deferred pay if a man assigns 50 per cent or more of his pay?

speechtext:
Would the minister
permit a supplementary question with respect to dependents' allowances? He probably has noticed my question on the order paper.
. Mr. RALSTON: I am getting off the subject mentioned by my hon. friend; may I deal with it for a moment? With regard to pay and allowances I can say, without being euphemistic at all, that these matters are receiving constant study and attention. I certainly will give his observations every possible study. I am not holding out any hope, but with the situation as presented there are some points in connection with pay and allowances which I feel should be corrected. Certainly I will take my hon. friend's suggestion into consideration.
May I say this-and I do not say it by way of defence at all-that I believe my hon. friend will find the pay and allowances of soldiers in Canada's army are at least as high as and probably higher than the pay and allowances in other armies.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Higher.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Probably. I have sent
out for the information with respect to Australia, but I believe with the possible exception of Australia our pay and allowances are higher than in any other army.
Then, the question of dependents' allowances follows directly after the statement I have just made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Before the minister leaves the question of pay and allowances,^ sometimes it is alleged that there is discrimination between the pay in the army and in the navy. I have had many representations to that effect. I have been told with respect to that matter that when one considers - the allowances received by men in the navy, which the men in the armed forces do not get, the pays are almost equivalent. However, I have never had that point demonstrated to me, if it is so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In that connection I
recall a conference I attended on that very subject when I held the portfolio of finance. Certain proposals were made with respect to the pay and allowances of one of the armed forces, and the treasury board insisted on what has just been suggested, namely a parity of the services. There is a difference in one respect with regard to pay in the navy, although I am sure I cannot remember the particulars now. I think, however, that when the pay and allowances are added up they will be found to be about on a parity. Possibly this is in the field of my colleague the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, but I shall be pleased to get the information.
I remember particularly one peculiar expression, namely an allowance for hard lying, which is awarded in the navy and not in the other services.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does that apply to the air force, too?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes, in the air force there are differences of pay, but not in equivalent ranks. It will be found there are a larger proportion of noncommissioned officers in the air force than in the army.
We are dealing now with the matter of dependents allowances. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar asked a question which is on the order paper, and with which I shall now deal. No doubt his quesion arises out of a report he saw in the press, with regard to action which has been taken by the dependents' allowance board in respect of the allowances to the wives of soldiers who had enlisted in the West Indies, who had come to Canada, but whose wives remained in the West Indies. In that case the dependents' allowance board apparently made an examination of the , cost of living in the West Indies as compared with the cost in Canada. The result was that they fixed the allowance payable to the wife at $20 instead of $35. A man with four children received allowances of $6, $6, $6 and $6 instead of $12, $12, $9 and $6. I may state frankly to the committee that the matter was brought to my attention

War Appropriation
when I was on the train going to the eastern coast; I had not heard of it before. In common with many hon. members, I believed that so far as a wife was concerned, in practice the allowance of $35 was inviolate, and that that amount was not to be disturbed. I can recall an occasion in the house when I was explaining the difference between the allowance payable to a mother and the allowance payable to a wife. I said then that the allowance payable to a wife was not disturbed or reduced, no matter how much the private income of the wife may have been. It was regarded as a matter of right. That was the way I believed it to be.
The matter was brought to my attention, and I immediately wrote the dependents' allowance board. I also wrote the correspondent who had written me. I have taken up the matter with the chairman of the dependents' allowance board and with the government. My position-and it is one which I know will be supported by the government, and carried out by the dependents' allowance board-is that notwithstanding the fact that the terms of the dependents' allowance regulation provide that the amount to be paid to a wife is such amount as the board may allow, not exceeding $35, at the same time in practice my feeling is that that amount should remain stationary, regardless of the cost of living of a particular individual who happens to be receiving the allowance. That rearrangement is being made. I have never taken that position with regard to the children. It does depend, I think, upon the cost of living, and there is no doubt whatever that the cost of living in the West Indies is very considerably less. I have not come to a decision in connection with that point, nor has the government. As a matter of fact I had not brought that part of it up because I was particularly concerned with the allowance to the wife.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You have not decided as to the children?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That has not been decided. It will be dealt with this week, as a matter of fact.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Has the minister decided the position of a wife drawing dependent's allowance and working for a department of the government? Is it possible now for a wife getting a dependent's allowance to work for a department of the government and not have her allowance decreased or diminished by virtue of such other employment?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Previously a wife who was in the employ of the government could not get dependent's allowance, but I think that has been remedied. I just want to be sure that it has been remedied in full and that there is not some relationship between the salary received and the dependent's allowance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Where a member of parliament is serving in the armed forces his wife receives no dependent's allowance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: This is the reverse.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think this ought to be decided upon some principle. Assuming that the wife of an enlisted man or an officer is in the employ of the government and getting $1,800 a year, any allowance paid to her would be based more on her marital status than any question of necessity. Certainly there could not be any argument that it was necessary. I think these cases should be looked into most carefully. I do not say that she should not have it, but certainly she is not as much entitled to it as a wife who is not in the employ of the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The answer to that is that the wife can obtain employment in a civil institution or private firm and receive her dependent's allowance and salary as well.

speechtext:
I am very glad to hear the minister's statement regarding the allowance to wives, and I hope that the same consideration will be given to the children. I feel this way about it, that if a man came from the West Indies, let us say, and volunteered for service in the Canadian forces, his family should be treated as our own Canadian families are treated. I am glad the minister takes the position he does, because I was afraid that this might extend to other parts of Canada where it might be claimed that the cost of living is lower than in some other places, and that we might reach right back on to the Indian reserves; we would then have a very complicated system of dependents' allowances.
There is dissatisfaction among the men in some quarters because they feel that the matter of leave is not sufficiently well regulated by the department itself. What I have in mind is this. At the end of six months a man may get, I understand, fourteen days' furlough. There are married men in, for example, the veterans guard. In some battalions or companies the commanding officer will allow men who are married and living home a day or two at a time as compassionate leave when they may go home and visit their families. There is provision for compassionate leave, I believe, in other respects. Some commanding officers give compassionate leave for sickness, or to attend to sickness at home, or whatever it may be, and make no deduction from the fourteen das's' furlough which is coming to them at the end of a period of time. In other places that compassionate leave is deducted from the fourteen days' furlough, with the result that men who, perhaps because of sickness in the home, have had compassionate leave, find at the end of six months that they have no further furlough coming to them, while in other cases the commanding officers are much more lenient and do not deduct the compassionate leave. In my opinion some policy should be stated, particularly for the married men in the veterans guard. I suggest that where compassionate allowance is given for family reasons-good and sufficient reasons -commanding officers should be instructed not to deduct that compassionate leave from the fourteen days that a man gets at the end of a given period-say six months; I am not just
sure on that point. Lack of uniformity in this matter sets a group ini one company against a group in another company; it discredits, perhaps, one commanding officer and makes another popular. The order in council is P.C. 6/1248 of February 18, 1941. It is a regulation made by the treasury board, not by the dependents' allowance board, and it is much more limited than I gave the committee to understand. The only persons who draw dependents' allowance if they are in the employ of the government are typists or stenographers grade 1, 1A or 2, laboratory workers in national research, employees of arsenals on munitions work, and in the inspection board. That this is a regulation, not of the dependents' allowance board but of the treasury board, indicates that the motivating reason for it was the necessity of getting female employees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would not the minister take that matter into consideration? Surely we should not penalize a woman who is a soldier's widow and perhaps the mother of two children in getting what work she can in the service of the state, or handicap her in comparison with those who can get work in an industrial concern. speechtext: I will take it into consideration. I am now only speculating as to what was behind the original regulation. I shall take it into consideration, but I would imagine the treasury board would consider it more from the point of view of getting man-power than from the point of view of changing the principle. It is now $25. They have
raised it? Yes, but both the $20 and the $5 are given only as a matter of charity, and there is a mass of red tape to go through. A man could get into the senate more easily than succeed in one of these cases. It is not right, and more than that it is a waste of time. I do not see why the woman should have to appear in jorma pauperis. I have heard this referred to as a "lousy" $5, and I have received enough letters to fill a cabinet. In one letter I was told by an official that I did not appreciate the situation, that even I should understand that the responsibility of a man towards his children is naturally greater than any responsibility he may have towards his brothers and sisters. This was a case where the man was the only support of his mother and three children and had gone to the war. They would not give the allowance. My answer was that I was not talking about responsibilities. I said that I was aware of the difference in responsibility between the case of a man supporting his children and the case where his responsibility was only towards brothers and sisters. I said I was talking about dependency, and that argument was not answered. I said that the dependency if it existed in one case was equal to that in the other, and indeed in some instances it is greater, for this reason, that a young, active woman can get around and chop her own firewood and do her own washing and things like that, whereas an old woman is unable to do these things and needs medicine and so on. So far as children are concerned, I cannot see that because a child happens to be a brother or a sister that fact makes it any cheaper to keep that child than if the child were the child of the soldier. I have been given different arguments, one of which was that they did it in Britain. I do not know what they do in Britain, but we are concerned with what is done here in Canada. Now, I want some justification which I can give to this widow and the children. I have to say to them, "You are in a different class.

War Appropriation
You may only get $20, or at most $25 handed out as charity, but the other person, the wife, can demand $35 by law." The minister said he was thoroughly convinced that wives should have as a basic sum $35 a month. I do want some explanation that I can take home to these people as to why dependent mothers are not treated in the same way. There are not so many, and Canada might afford it. It is not a matter whether he is responsible or not. The question is one of dependency and the government have admitted a certain amount of dependency. If the question is one of dependency, why not give her the same sum as the wife can claim as of right?

speechtext:
May I
add a word to that. Yesterday I was talking on t'he train to a young man who told me his story. Fifteen years ago he came from Glasgow, and he married his sweetheart also from Glasgow. They did not get along and she went home and he has not seen her for twelve years. She has never come back. Two children were born and his mother, who is a widow, took them after the wife left. This man enlisted. He had been earning $18 a week in a cotton mill-I forget what he was doing-and he was told that she would get $20 a month assigned pay, which was his, $20 dependents' allowance, and so much for each child. He assigned his pay and the mother gets so much for each child. She has never been able to get dependents' allowance although he was, I understand, the sole support of the family. It may be that twelve years ago his mother was able to work-I do not know about that-but the fact is that the dependents' allowance board draws a sharp distinction between the wife and the mother. Their rights are in entirely different categories. The wife has a legal right to support by her husband; the mother's right to support is based on another principle. My hon. friend objects to the words ex necessitate; he translates that into charity. I do not think it is quite that. Certainly the mother has not the legal right that the wife has, and that has been recognized in a degree; there is a discrimination in the amount. I am not objecting to the discrimination; there is a basic difference between the two.
All these cases of mothers' allowances and dependents' allowances cause members of parliament a great deal of trouble. They cause me much trouble, but fortunately I have somebody to help me. I should like the minister to give consideration to the question of the widowed mother who takes the burden in a case such as the one I have mentioned. The children of the enlisted
soldier are in a different category from brothers and sisters of an enlisted man. Certainly he is legally as well as morally responsible for the support of his own children. I do not think there is the same obligation for the support of his brothers and sisters.

speechtext:
The passage in Hansard to which reference has been made will be found at page 205-06 of May 24, 1940. I am not sure that the question that has been asked was not answered then. The leader of the opposition has indicated the distinction. All I can say further is that in all pension legislation-and this applies to disability pensions as well, after the man has been discharged-so far as I know there has been a straight line of distinction between the basis of assessment for the mother and that for the wife. The wife being the direct dependent, literally, of the husband is entitled as of right to the amount which is set out in the statute; that is to say, in practice, whether or not the statute may be mandatory or permissive. The rule has always been that the wife was entitled to a pension of a certain amount regardless of her own income or her financial position. What applies to the mother applies also to the father, and I would point out that if my hon. friend's argument applies to the mother it applies to the father as well, and the father would be entitled as being in the category of dependents. He would be a dependent, regardless of how much income he might have, on the ground that his son was in the army. The right of the mother depends altogether on this question: Of what has she been deprived financially by reason of the enlistment of her son in the army? What the country does is to try to make up to her financially the support of which she has been deprived to the extent to which her son has been supporting her. That is a clear distinction, and the principle is altogether different from that on which the allowance is made to the wife. Certain cases arose, which the committee will recall, in which the son would have supported the mother had he been able to do so but he had been prevented by reasons beyond his control, and an amendment was made to the dependents' allowance regulations to provide that the board could ascertain whether or not, in their opinion, the son would have
War Appropriation

supported the mother had he been able to do so; and if they found that was so, they made provision for her to the amount which would have been contributed had he been in a position to contribute. Now that is exactly the same practice, on all fours with the provisions of the Pension Act providing for dependents of soldiers after their discharge, and I think it has worked very well. It does of course require the assessment of the means of the soldier and of the needs of the mother, which is not required in connection with the wife, but it is a principle which has been in every piece of pension legislation that I know anything about. I think it is manifestly equitable because it endeavours to make up to the mother the financial loss she may have incurred by reason of the son's enlistment.

I wanted to say a few words while we were still on the question of dependents' allowances. There are many ramifications to the minister's department, and I think it would be well if we kept to one question at a time and endeavoured to settle it.
There is a matter in connection with dependents' allowances which I brought to the attention of the minister last year and which I want to bring to his attention again. Personally I find that this is causing considerable hardship on dependents; I am referring to the men who go absent without leave. After a man is absent without leave for twenty-one days he is posted as a deserter, and his pay and the dependents' allowances are cut off. As I see it, the man is not punished at all, except by being confined to the guard room. He is fed; he 's clothed; he is kept comfortable, and he has no worries. Majesty's government feel therefore that in addition to the improvements announced above and to the revised war service grants scheme introduced in October, 1941, some financial aid should now be provided for other rank members of the forces against the needs which will arise in the period of post-war readjustment.
They therefore propose to introduce a system of post-war credits for the forces which will be of a simple and straightforward character. Under this system there will be set aside for all ratings and other ranks a sum of 6d. in respect of every day of paid service from the 1st January, 1942. In the case of the women's forces the sum will be 4d. per day, following the two-thirds principle adopted for basic pay and war pay. The sums so set aside will be accumulated and will be made available to the individuals concerned after the war and after discharge from the forces.
The method of payment of the credits will follow that which is to be adopted in the case of the special credits associated with the increases in the income tax made in the last budget-i.e. they will be made available to the individual in the form of a deposit in the post office savings bank (or in such other institutions as may be approved for the income tax scheme).
Why would it not be possible in Canada to provide these credits in the form of war bonds or war saving certificates which could be held for the fighting men?
The white paper concludes:
Arrangements will be made for the credits to be specially released to persons invalided out of the forces or to the estate in the event of death.
The minister has explained this afternoon that Canada goes part of the way along that road, in that ^he holds back some pay from those of our men who do not assign any of their pay, but I suggest that we go much further and make an extra payment to all our men in the form of a post-war credit, much in the manner that the British government has done.
The second suggestion is that steps should be taken to extend the wartime housing work so that it will help the dependents of these men in the forces. That scheme was initiated last year, but the Minister of Munitions and Supply explained on March 7 that it was meant only to help men in war industry. As reported in Hansard, page 1454, he said:
I should like to emphasize that this is not a general housing project but is confined solely to housing that is found necessary for the successful prosecution of the munitions programme.
He repeated the same statement last fall, when he said, as reported at page 4229:
These houses are entirely for the purpose of housing munitions workers.
Well, this position has arisen, that soldiers' dependents are being forced into the poorer houses. There is a demand for houses to rent, and as higher wages are being paid to civilian workers the soldier's wife goes down the scale

and is forced to rent poorer and poorer accommodation. I suggest that the work of Wartime Housing Limited be extended so that some provision can be made for the dependents of men in the fighting forces. These dependents should have suitable living quarters at a low rental, and now is the time to get busy on providing them with that type of accommodation.
The third suggestion is that Canada should pay an allowance for all the children of the man in the fighting forces. In Great Britain they do that. The scale of pay there is seven shillings and sixpence per week for the first child, five shillings and sixpence for the second child, four shillings for the third child and for any subsequent child. In Canada at the outbreak of war the government adopted a policy of paying an allowance for only two children, the idea being to restrict the enlistment of men with more than two children. I have never been able to see the wisdom in that policy, because the man with more than two children was allowed to enlist, but when he had enlisted no allowance was paid for more than two children. That in effect made his dependents pay the shot for his enlist ment. I believe the policy was based on the wrong line of thought. The Minister of Finance repeated the same policy last fall when he announced that Canada would pay an additional allowance for the third and fourth child. He used these words in stating, at page 4424 of Hansard, that the government would not pay for more than four children: -because we believe that definite steps should be taken to discourage the recruiting of men with large families.
The fair way to handle the problem, if it is a problem, would be to say, "We will not take any men who have more than four children." Then there could be no hardship suffered by the wife and the children. But if the government does not wish to do that,
I suggest that it follow the British practice and pay an allowance for all the children, no matter how many there may be.

The fourth and final suggestion has to do with a cost of living bonus for the dependents. That has been covered fully already by other speakers this afternoon, so I shall not take any time on it other than to say this. Canadian wage earners are getting this bonus as a matter of right. It is not a question of dragging a wage earner before some board and finding out whether his family are hard up or whether there is some other reason why he should get the bonus. He gets that bonus as a right; and in my opinion the members of the fighting forces should be placed in the same position-their dependents should get the cost of living bonus as of right. At the present time an increase is given only in the hardship cases, which means that there is a means test, and that, I submit, is not the proper procedure to follow.
Those are the four suggestions. Many others might be made, and I would urge private members not to be bashful in bringing forward proposals for the improvement of the lot of the fighting men and their dependents. Some will say that changes like these cost money. That is quite true. But I thought that great Canadian, Stephen Leacock, put the situation very clearly in one of his articles which advocated equal pay for the fighting men, when he stated, towards the end of the article;
But even if it looks too great a financial burden we must pick it up anyway. We who can do so little while they go to do so much, have no choice. Surely we can face a deficit for those who face death.
I appeal to hon. members to bear in mind those three words, "equality of sacrifice", at all times when questions of this type are being considered, and I should like to suggest to them that at all times our main concern in this house should be to help and take care of these fighting men and their dependents.

The members of this group would like to associate themselves with the other hon. members who have pressed upon the minister consideration of the cost of living bonus to dependents. We raised this question last year. I do not want to labour it again now, but certainly it is worthy of consideration. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) said that the general cost of living had gone up 15 per cent since the beginning of the war. One of the western newspapers made a survey last August in the stores in the city of Winnipeg of the thirty-eight commodities which people buy most commonly in these stores-that is, the things which the common people buy. It was found that on these commodities the cost of living had gone up at that time 22 per
cent since August 1939. There is no doubt that the woman who is supporting a small family and whose husband is overseas has actually less purchasing power to-day in her allowance than the purchasing power which she received when her husband first joined the army. I hope the government will give consideration to this matter.
I want to ask the minister two questions; they are not related, but I thought I would double them up together because a number of hon. members will want to ask the minister questions. The first is with relation to the men overseas. I have had letters from a number of men overseas, and with hardly a single exception they have all mentioned the same thing with regard to the question of living allowance when they get leave overseas. A part of their pay is deferred. I was under the impression that all had some part of their pay deferred irrespective of how much earned pay they had, but the minister says that is not correct. These men had a certain amount of pay deferred and received only a small part of their pay. It took nearly all of that pay to buy necessities such as cigarettes, shaving materials and so on, and when they were granted leave they were not given any living allowance. I understand that in the British forces some living allowance is granted. These men I am speaking of are not given any, and a number of them actually found that it was better to stay in camp, but then they discovered that they could not stay in camp because the quartermaster's stores did not assign supplies for them on the ground that they were not on the roster for those particular days. For that reason they could not remain in camp. The complaint was that a good many of them who got leave would have liked to go to London or Glasgow but could not do so unless they could borrow money from their comrades or make other arrangements. Will the minister give consideration to that? I am citing the facts as they have been given to me in correspondence. The minister can check them up.
The other matter I want to mention has no relation to pay and allowances. I wish to raise the question of what coordination is taking place in the Canadian army that is being set up in England. One of the greatest military problems which the united nations have faced is that of unification or coordination of command. In reading Lord Gort's report, one of the things with which the reader was impressed was not only the lack of air power during those fateful days when France fell, but the fact that the commander in chief did not have the control and disposition of that air power because the Royal Air Force was under a

War Appropriation

different command. The escape of the Gneisenau and the Schamhorst a few weeks ago raised the same question in Great Britain. There they had three general staffs, and there was a feeling that there was not sufficient coordination and there might be need for complete unification of command. There is no doubt that if the Canadian troops go into a theatre of war, their success and indeed the lives of the men will depend to a large extent upon the amount of air support they get and whether or not the commander in chief has at his disposal that air support.
In the Canadian army under General McNaughton, will the Royal Canadian Air Force operating there be under his command or under the command of the Royal Air Force? Will he have, as army commander, control and disposition of the Canadian air forces, or will he depend upon the general staff of the Royal Air Force for such air support as they care to place at his disposal from time to time? That is important. No one doubts-and we say it with pride-that if operations are opened in Europe, the Canadian troops will be in all probability in the vanguard, and we owe it to these men and to their chances of success to see to it that they have the best type of air support and that there is complete synchronization in all branches of the service. That is possible only if the commander an chief has some voice and has under his command complete control of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
Would the minister now tell the committee about the new organization that is being set up in Britain in connection with the Canadian army under General McNaughton; what will be the position of the commander in chief with respect to the Royal Canadian Air Force, whether they will be under his command or whether they will continue under the Royal Air Force? Will General McNaughton depend upon them for such support as they choose to give from time to time?

I have inquired whether it is done for the United Kingdom forces and am unable to get the information at the moment. I shall inquire into the matter. My hon. friend will, however,
