realize that rates of pay for United Kingdom forces are far different from our own. Nothing illustrates that better than the figures given by the hon. member for Vancouver South. For instance, a dependents' allowance of 7/6 per week for the first child would come to about $5 a month in Canadian funds, whereas our amount is $12. 'I mention that only to indicate that what is done for the United Kingdom forces in a matter of that kind would not be a precedent for us having regard to the very much larger amount of our pay and allowances. I shall, however, look into the situation with a view to giving it consideration along with these other matters.
Cost of living bonus has been dealt with. All I can say is that the measure announced by the Minister of Finance, the appointment of the dependents' trustee board, was intended to provide for cases where the dependents' allowance did not cover the situation and, as the minister frankly told the house and the country, the idea was not to make a uniform increase but to deal with cases on their merits.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Individual cases.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Individual cases, because it was felt that the $35 paid1 the wife-and I cite this in support of my contention that the $35 should be $35-was being paid already, and therefore any addition to that caused by increased cost of living could be taken care of by the dependents' board of trustees. It would revolutionize the whole system of pay for soldiers and dependents if this were adopted. It would mean the scrapping of the dependents' board of trustees altogether and the dependents' allowances regulations. If that is the proper thing to do, nothing is impossible. I have made a note of the point in connection with the other matters to which reference has been made.
The hon. member for Vancouver South mentioned allowances for all children instead of only four. That was very carefully thought of and1 studied at the time the amendments were made. The allowances are $12 for the first child, $12 for the second, $9 for the third and $6 for the fourth, and without being facetious I think a man in England would have to have quite a family before he would approach in the aggregate the amount here, namely $39.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think the minister will admit that is not a very fair comparison because the cost of living is quite different there.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I was in Great Britain lately and I must say the cost of living that I experienced there is not much different.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But these people cannot live at the best hotels.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend's suggestion in a word is, allowances for all children. I agree with my hon. friend in this, that personally I am not in accord with the idea that a man should be discouraged from enlisting because he has a large family.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They still take them in even if a man has a dozen children.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is right. A man in my own constituency has ten boys. Seven are in the army; two are on the waiting list now for the navy and air force, and the last is being called up. That is not a bad contribution.
With regard to housing, that is a problem which has concerned me more than anything else. If we could settle that, it would be a tremendous relief all across this country among dependents of service men. The ground taken by my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply in regard to the Wartime Housing Act was that these men going to work in industry were moving in and becoming part of the establishment and these houses were being built as part of the plant. On the other hand, a soldier's wife presumably has a residence some place; she does not necessarily have to move, and therefore the provision she had should be sufficient. The complaints that come to me are not quite the same as those coming to the hon. member for Vancouver South, to the effect conditions are getting poorer and poorer because of the lack of dependents' allowances or ability to pay. I think the dependents' allowances permit them to pay rent if the houses are available, but what comes to me is that landlords are not enthusiastic about taking soldiers' wives; some are defintely reluctant.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is the scarcity of houses.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The idea is they had a
house when the husband enlisted.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is sold over their
heads.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The landlord has rented
it to some one else. We have not been taking on the question of housing because I have not felt that it was our responsibility. It is a financial matter and a national matter which has to do with housing conditions in Canada generally, not with soldiers' wives alone.
War Appropriation

What I have done-and my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply has been very cooperative about it-is to endeavour to get for the benefit of municipalities the use of ten or twenty or more houses in order that they may use them temporarily as at least a stopping place for soldiers' families who are moving. I must take this position- it is the position taken by my colleague the Minister of Finance-that this question of housing the citizens of Canada-not people moving transiently-is the problem of the municipalities rather than that of the federal government. I have appealed on a number of occasions to bodies in different towns who were anxious to do war work, and have received most heartening response; I said, "you can help by taking under your wing soldiers' families who are having difficulty, acting as big brother and getting them places to live"; and that has been done with the assistance of these houses temporarily loaned by Wartime Housing Limited. The problem is perplexing; we have not overlooked it. I know the situation in regard to the navy is very much the same; I have not heard so much about the air force. Whether anything can be done from the point of view of the service departments I am not able to say at the moment, but we have it under active study and attention.
Post-war credits are really the same principle as the deferred pay suggested by the hon. member for Peel, which I promised to look into. I notice the amount in the United Kingdom is sixpence a day, which is not very much translated into Canadian dollars, something like $25 or $30 a year. War savings certificates would probably be more appropriate than war bonds.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is there any arrangement whereby the dependent of a man who has enlisted in the forces of a friendly allied nation could receive dependents' allowance? I have had drawn to my attention the dependent of a man Who enlisted in the Netherlands army, and his wife would like to know whether she is eligible to receive dependents' allowance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No; she would not be eligible, but from what I know of our friends from Holland I am sure she would be looked after. She would not be eligible to receive the dependents' allowance from Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is their responsibility?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Is there not some way in which the government could do something .about these cases? Last year, of course, the

friendly allied governments were not allowed to exercise compulsion on their nationals in this country. I understand that more recently an order in council has been passed giving them power to call up their nationals resident in Canada. If those nationals are called up, then would it not be proper, in giving these governments that power, also to stipulate that something should be done for their dependents? Otherwise those dependents are going to be the recipients of relief in this country. Some arrangements should be entered into by the governments .concerned so that the dependents of men subject to call by the allied governments in exile would be protected to the extent of some living allowance. Would the minister look into that matter?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I shall be very glad to do so, though really it is a matter for the Department of External Affairs.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We in this corner would like to associate ourselves with the remarks of those who have been urging an increase in pay and allowances, and also with those who have been requesting free transportation for furloughs and embarkation leaves. I am not going to labour those matters at this time, because we have taken a consistent stand in connection with them.
There is something else I should like to mention, a matter which I do not think has been referred to this afternoon. Earlier in the day the minister stated that he believed the dependents' allowance should be kept inviolate.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No; I thought the $35 payable to the wife should not be reduced on account of the cost of living.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am wondering how the minister would justify the passing of order in council P.C. 138, 1936, which gives the soldier settlement board the right to attach a certain portion of the wife's allowance, not exceeding $20 a month. I would point out that the wife of the soldier is in the position that she has to hire a man to do the work her husband was doing; and for that reason, if for no other, she will need the allowance to pay this man's wages. The argument is advanced by the soldier settlement board that the amount seized would not be greater than the rent the wife would have to pay for the house in other circumstances. I would point out that the soldier settlement board have no more right to take that stand than a mortgage company holding a mortgage on a farm would have. The soldier enlists; the wife is left on the farm. The mortgage company would be equally justified in asking permission to

War Appropriation
attach the dependents' allowance for the purpose of charging that woman rent; or a storekeeper would have just as much right to say that he should be allowed to attach the dependents' allowance for the store bill. I cannot see why the soldier settlement board should be given this special privilege. They argue, of course, that it helps pay off the debt of the soldier settler, but exactly the same argument could be advanced by any private creditor, by a mortgage company or by a storekeeper. I was wondering what justification the minister could suggest for the passing of that order in council.
It is hardly necessary for me to point out to the minister that this action destroys the principle of section 118 of the allowance regulations, which states that the dependents' allowance cannot be attached. It also destroys the principle of section 98, which states that the allowance is for the purpose of promoting the well-being and efficiency of the military forces of Canada by providing that means to alleviate the financial anxiety of members with respect to the domestic welfare of dependents, while they are in the service of his majesty. I would point out that if there is one class of society in this country that is in financial difficulties, it is the soldier settlers. Certainly it is not going to relieve the anxiety in the mind of a soldier to know that a certain portion of the allowance is being seized instead of going to his wife. Would the minister say a few words in that connection?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I was not in the house at the time, but I believe my hon. friend brought up that point the other night when my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources was in his place, and I believe the minister made a somewhat extended reference by way of explanation of the provision.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He just took an individual case and justified it. He said in that case the dependent had seven children and was receiving a large allowance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have sent for a copy of Hansard containing that discussion. I intended to discuss the matter with my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources. My hon. friend has been very fair about it; I think he has given the reasons which the soldier settlement board give for taking this action. The principal reason that struck me was the fact that they were not charging any more than the rent that would have to be paid if the farm were leased, and under those circumstances it did seem that there was no hardship and nothing improper in asking that this amount be paid. I have not had a chance to
discuss the matter with my colleague, but I intend to deal with it more thoroughly and will talk to him about it. I am not in ; position, in view of the explanation which my hon. friend makes, to say that any change will be made, but certainly I shall look into the matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I suppose the technical question of a crown debt has some influence on the treasury.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. Just on that point the section which my hon. friend quoted, which indicated that the allowance was not garnishable or attachable, does not apply in a case of this kind.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the question of the hospitalization of dependents of soldiers. Quite a number of soldiers are getting into financial difficulties through having to pay hospital bills for their dependents. Not only are they creating hardship for themselves; they are creating hardship for many of the hospitals in the smaller communities. This matter has been brought to my attention in regard to the Nanaimo camp. The hospital at Nanaimo is now some $6,000 in arrears on account of soldiers' dependents being hospitalized there, and I am wondering whether there is not some way of taking care of this load for the men in uniform.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is in connection with the dependents?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is a new thought.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. I do not think I am prepared to say anything more, but I will have the matter examined. I think it must be a special case, of a large camp near a small town with limited hospital facilities, but I am just a little concerned about hospital bills-which I am sure must be reasonable- not being paid. Or is there a particular epidemic among the dependents of soldiers out there, which means that a large number of them are becoming ill?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If the hon. member will allow me, in my province the matter is taken care of by law. If the dependent of a soldier is in need of hospitalization and that person goes to hospital and is unable to pay, the municipality pays as a matter of law and a matter of course. That is the way I think it ought to be. It is not a charity; it is a community duty which is performed by the municipality under a well considered and well regulated practice.
War Appropriation

Mr.- MAYHEW: In British Columbia the municipalities pay so much and the provincial government pays so much, but there is something left which the patient is supposed to pay. That accounts for the amount left unpaid in this case. We talk about equal sacrifices. I think at least we have arrived at the point where we know we cannot make equal sacrifices, but I think we can do a great deal more to share the burdens of the soldiers. We are not doing it as far as hospitalization is concerned. Whether it should come from this government or from the municipalities or from any other source, it should not be a matter of passing the buck and leaving the soldiers stranded with a load of debt on account of their wives or children.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I wonder whether that would not fee taken care of by the trustees of the dependents' allowance board?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If they can go far enough.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If my hon. friend has a case in mind I shall bring it to the attention of the chairman of the board of trustees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes; I have a list of sixty or seventy cases from the Nanaimo hospital alone.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The observations of the leader of the opposition are quite correct. I happen to be chairman of a hospital in Ontario, and I know that the governments of the province, the county and the municipality pay the full cost of indigent patients. No cost is charged to the patient if he is indigent.
Mr. CO'LDWELL:	But are soldiers
indigents?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does the hon. member call a soldier an indigent person?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I was just talking about the cost they could not take care of themselves.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: As the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, has pointed out, the distinction is that the wives and dependents of soldiers cannot be considered as indigent charity cases. They deserve something better than the poor law. That is practically what is done in New Brunswick, Ontario and, I may say, my own province of Saskatchewan. But the thing is wrong. Surely these peolpe are entitled to better treatment than the ordinary charity case in a municipal or other hospital.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The law in British Columbia is that the municipalities are called upon to pay seventy-five cents or a dollar a day, and the government pays a like amount. But that does not deter the hospital from sending a hospital bill to the patient.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: This is not a question of the application of the principle of the poor law. It is a question of policy on the part of the civil authorities in a province or municipality. They must decide how people who cannot pay, whether they be dependents of soldiers or others, are to be cared for. If they can pay they are asked to pay, and if they cannot pay they are not asked to pay. No one who is not able to pay gets a bill. I am not prepared to say whether it is the responsibility of the government, but I know in my own province it is taken care of by the community. It is a community service and community obligation, and is in no sense a reflection on any of the recipients. If the suggestion is made in a derogatory sense, it is entirely out of place. It is community service rendered by reason of enlightened public opinion crystallized into law.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Many of the men in these camps come from provinces which have not laws similar to those in British Columbia or New Brunswick. Therefore there is no compensation for part of their keep. It must all come from the portion paid by the provincial government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There is a residence qualification.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, there is a residence qualification.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I presume the Minister of National Defence has under his jurisdiction dependents' allowances for all the services- the air force, the navy and the army.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The navy has a special set of regulations mentioned in the orders.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does the dependents' allowance board deal with them?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The dependents' allowance
board- comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Defence.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, but I try to keep my hands off the dependents' allowance board entirely. The only time I ever interfered with it in the slightest was with respect to a discussion of policy raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. That matter was discussed in a letter to which I referred. I do not know that I can help the hon. member much with respect to the navy or the air force.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: With whom, then, should we take up these matters?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
They should be taken up with the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, if they are naval matters.

War Appropriation

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He is in a position to say that this comes under the dependents' allowance board, and the dependents' allowance board comes under-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I made the recommendations with regard to the appointment of the dependents' allowance board, originally. But dependents' allowances for the navy are under naval regulations. Naval pay and allowance regulations are quite separate from army pay and allowance and air force pay and allowance regulations. Each service has a liaison with the dependents' allowance board; each service has a member on the board, so that my hon. friend would probably get better service and better information, if he has in mind a matter concerned with the naval service, if he would take it up with the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, who would have communication with the naval member on the board. The same would be true with respect to the Minister of National Defence for Air. However, I should be pleased to make a note of any case to which my hon. friend might refer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I was going to ask someone to make a statement with regard to the great disparity between dependents' allowances for members of the navy, and those of the army and the air force.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I will get all the information I can. But as I said a little while ago, the whole matter of pay and allowances was discussed by a joint committee. There is an interservice committee on pay and allowances which is considering these matters constantly. I believe the feeling was that they had pretty well arrived at a parity with regard to allowances, in view of existing conditions. However, if there is any point my hon. friend wishes to bring up, or any particular ranks he would like to compare, I will see that they are compared, and that reasons are given why one rate of pay is paid in one case and another rate in another.
As indicated by the leader of the opposition, the general principle was that taking it in the aggregate-that is to say, pay plus allowances -you arrived generally at a parity. There are some cases, more particularly in the navy, where they prefer their system to the systems used by the army and the air force.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have some figures with respect to differences between the army and the navy. It appears, so far as commissioned ranks are concerned, that exactly the same amount is paid to the wife of a naval sub-lieutenant as is paid to the wife of a naval commander, namely, 830. The army position equivalent to the naval sub-lieutenant is that of the army
lieutenant, and his wife is paid $45. The wife of the army lieutenant-colonel, who is the equivalent of a naval commander, receives $60.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What about the pay?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The pay of a naval lieutenant is $4 a day, whereas that of an army lieutenant is $5 a day. Consequently the total amount received by a naval sub-lieutenant, including pay and allowances, is $150 a month, as compared with an army lieutenant at $195 a month.
There is not such a great distinction in the higher ranks. However, the army lieutenant-colonel obtains a total of $360 a month pay and allowances, whereas the naval commander obtains $330 a month.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Both married and with children?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am speaking of married men without children.
The minister made some statement with respect to men who are missing. He said it was the policy in the army that pay and allowances would be continued1 until some evidence had been found that a soldier was dead, or could be presumed dead. The presumption of death is arrived at after a period of six months.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is the hon. member asking me that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am making that statement; that is the way I understand- it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not think I mentioned six months.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No; I am saying that. I understand there is a presumption of death after six months following the notice indicating that a soldier is missing. Who determines that policy? Is it the Department of National Defence in connection with a soldier, the Department of National Defence for Naval Services in connection with a seaman and the Department of National Defence for Air in connection with the air force?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The offices corresponding to the adjutant-general's branch in the army determine it for the navy and air force respectively.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is there any way in which there could be worked out a coordinated policy in that connection between the various services?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If there is a time when the fur gets up on the back of my neck it is when someone mentions coordination. We are
War Appropriation

working out coordination constantly; we have interservice committees. For instance, we have a pay and allowances committee. Some things are different in the three services. Each service likes to do things its own way, but I do not think it makes any great difference which way it is done when it comes to the rate of pay. If the army are satisfied with their rates and practice as they are and always have been, and if the navy has a different practice in that connection and is satisfied with it, it does not seem to me that there is any particular public advantage in pounding their heads together and saying, "you must accept this other system." There are some traditions in connection with these services. I think the answer to my hon. friend's question is that there is coordination by means of the defence council and the interservice committee on pay and allowances. There is an interservice committee which has to do with personnel conditions. We try as best we can to have coordination, which is not necessarily absolute uniformity. I think we should distinguish between the two.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: As a matter of fact what I had down was "uniform policy"; I did not intend to use the word "coordination." I am pleased to have the minister make the statement he did, that pay and allowances are to be continued in the army in the manner in which they are. I am particularly concerned with the air force, because it is in connection with that force that we have so many men missing. If a man is listed as missing in the middle of the month, his pay is paid for the balance of that month, but after that it drops down to the $60 a month his wife would get in case of his death. I do not see why a distinction should be made between the services in respect of a thing like that. At the same time, his child is continued at the lower rate, namely $12 a month, and is not raised to the $15 a month which would be paid if he were officially declared dead. It seems to me that the same policy should be adopted with respect to the air force as is followed in the other services. A wife who receives information that her husband is missing should not have the additional blow of having her income reduced automatically.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If I could I would be very glad to give my hon. friend an explanation, but it would be the merest guess and would not be informative. I would prefer that he take the matter up with my colleague, the Minister of National Defence for Air. It may be that they are following the practice of the Royal Air Force with which they are closely associated.
flVlr. Ralston.]

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The matter of the decision in regard to the payment of hospitalization of dependents was not cleared up to my satisfaction, although I may have failed to grasp what was said. As it was left in my mind, the only disposition made was that suggested by the leader of the opposition, that the municipality should pay. What information has the minister regarding that matter?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The way I dealt with
it was to indicate that the dependents' board of trustees, which was established in November or December, has as one of its functions and one of its authorities, to pay such supplementary grants or to give such special assistance in those cases where it is satisfied that such supplementary grants or special assistance are necessary to prevent hardships arising because of unusual circumstances or to relieve misfortune and meet domestic emergencies, including serious illness of a member of the family. If the hospitalization which was referred to could not be handled by the soldier himself, I think it would come within that provision. I am not at this moment saying that the country should simply undertake the hospitalization of all the soldier's family. We must have regard for certain general principles. I am saying, however, that if the soldier is unable to take care of it, there is a provision which it seems to me could be made applicable and which seems, in terms at least, to be amply sufficient for the purpose.

I would say that
the idea behind the; minister's proposal is more sound than the idea behind the suggestion of the leader of the opposition. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In the artillery training camps have we any modem guns for practice purposes? For instance, it is represented to me that at Petawawa there is not a modern gun, and that they are using for training purposes old 18-pounders of the last war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not know whether the Minister of National Defence has made any comment with respect to a question which I should like to ask him at this time. I understand that prior to the Easter recess he was giving sympathetic consideration to the proposal that the government should advance loans to medical students who are attending the various Canadian universities, to enable them to continue their studies, provided, of course, that they undertake to join the Canadian army medical corps. During the recess I discussed the matter with some of these students, and they were in a quandary as to what the department intended to do. I wish the minister would make a statement on this matter, because some of the universities are closing, and others will close in a very short time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I made a statement on this subject in the house about four weeks ago or perhaps a little more. The provisions with regard to the assistance were, first, that men who undertook to give their services in the national effort would be assisted, where the need existed, by the Department of Labour, who would give them scholarships. For the last two years those who enlisted would be given leave with pay and permitted to continue their studies. We had meetings with representatives of the universities. They have concurred in the plan, and the orders have actually gone out to the universities. As a matter of fact, I have myself signed a letter to either the deans of the medical faculties or to the presidents of the universities themselves, outlining the plan. In addition,

TFor Appropriation

the regulations were completed recently; I am told that they would have reached the universities about three days ago. Those regulations give full details as to what these young men should do. I think the matter is now wholly in order, and that the universities understand the procedure thoroughly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Have any of the universities refused to accept the proposals?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No-none of the medical schools. There are medical schools in only a certain number of the universities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to the rehabilitation of men. I will put this case. A young man of very good education, bilingual, of French ofigin, teaching in an academic course in the maritime provinces, enlisted in the air force, was taken to the manning depot, and from there transferred to the air school, where he taught certain subjects connected with aeronautics. While there, it was discovered that he had a hernia; and he was to be transferred to the army for a course, on the theory that he would get hospitalization and have an operation-which I believe is very simple-and would then go into the infantry. I am now informed that no provision is made for hospitalization of this sort, and he is not able to afford the operation himself. I think I have read that some provision is made for the physical rehabilitation of men under such conditions. This man is of a very fine type, and I believe that if he could be rehabilitated physically he would be a valuable officer because of his bilingual qualifications; I understand that such men are all too scarce. What is the position with reference to a case like that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The case my hon. friend
cites is exactly the sort which the regulations and the policy announced a short time ago were intended to cover. There could only be one possible "out" in connection with it, and that would be if the officer or man referred to was too old; that is to say, that the doctors would not consider that a hernia operation would be sufficient to mend him to pass army requirements. My hon. friend is right in assuming that there is provision for such a case as that. The provision is that he is handed over to the Department of Pensions and National Health. I do not mean that we are shelving the responsibility, but that is the department which actually does the operation.
[Mr. Ralston.!

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I shall
be glad to send the minister particulars of the case if he has not already received them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I would appreciate it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: A few nights ago the minister intimated that it was the intention of his department to set up on the west coast a school for the purpose of training inspectors in the development of commando troops. Is there any .particular reason why that school should be set up on the west coast? If it is the intention to train troops for that purpose, and to establish a school, would it not be more economical, more in the general interests of the country, and serve a greater purpose if it were located more centrally? I presume some would be taken from the east coast for that purpose. Taking them from one end of the country to the other seems a rather silly operation, and I think the school might be established somewhere in the centre of Canada because it would then serve the whole dominion to greater advantage.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Consideration along that
line has been going on for some time. The primary reason for considering the west coast-it was not necessarily the west coast, although I said the west-was the fact that conditions there prevail all the year round and are better for training than they are in the east. Moreover, at the present time we have a great many military establishments in the east.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Before the dinner
recess we were dealing with the matter of the health of dependents. Discussing this question a short time ago, a number of us came to the conclusion that it might be a good idea for the department to lay out some sort of plan whereby a form of state medicine or state health insurance might be provided for all dependents of soldiers. That might be extended to take in a number of old age pensioners, of whom we have so many in various parts of our province. A constructive suggestion that occurred to us was this. This is one branch of the minister's work that might be handed over to the Minister of Pensions and National Health. It would act as a proving ground for the question of state medicine on a small scale and we might learn some interesting and instructive facts from the experiment.
Then, would the minister give an outline of the steps that are taken to ensure that members of the armed forces shall receive supplies and equipment which are up to standard. What steps are taken by the Department of National Defence to inspect technical equipment? Are munitions, tanks,

War Appropriation
small arms, anti-aircraft guns and so on tested in Canada before shipments are made to our forces in other parts of the world?
A third matter which I would discuss for just a moment is that of seeing that men are placed in occupations in which they can do the most effective work in the forces. We saw a number of enlistment advertisements in which men were asked to join the armed forces. They were calling for tradesmen, and on one visit to the camp last year I ran across a man who had entered as a butcher and was then in the hospital, while a blacksmith was serving as a cook and a medical orderly was working as provost. In the early days of organization, of course, there must be some confusion; but would the minister give us a statement as to what is being done to ensure that men are being used in the armed forces in those occupations in which they were previously trained?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With regard to the first question respecting health insurance for dependents, I have learned enough in my short career not to step into the field of other departments if that can be avoided. It is part of my responsibility in an indirect way, in connection with the welfare of the soldiers, to assist with regard to their dependents. But health insurance is a matter for two other departments, namely, the Department of Pensions and National Health, as my hon. friend has suggested, and the Department of Finance, under which the superintendent of insurance operates. I will bring the matter to the attention of these two departments. I will not say any more at this stage with regard to it.
So far as the matter of inspection is concerned, I could speak at length in reference to what I know of the organization; but let me say briefly that after-inspection is carried out by the joint inspection board of the United Kingdom and Canada under the direction of Major-General Locke, who came here early in the war, and is himself not only a most competent and capable organizer, but has a thorough technical knowledge of arms and equipment and the munitions which are being turned out. The board has employees running into thousands, both in Canada and in the United States, and every type of equipment and munitions is inspected by the board before it is accepted by the Department of National Defence or, for that matter, by the British government. I can assure the committee that nothing is left undone in the way of inspection and testing. I know of a number of proving grounds which they have, and tests are carried out. As a matter of fact, for our own satisfaction, these tests are supplemented or are preceded by tests with
44561-124J
pilot models made by the master-general of the ordnance, who is the provision officer of the Department of National Defence. The board has expanded rapidly and is most capable and efficient, the organization consisting of personnel who know their job thoroughly.
With regard to the question of personnel, since the committee was last discussing the resolution I have had an opportunity of a long discussion with the director of personnel selection at headquarters, Brigadier Chisholm, who has charge of the personnel selection branch, and I incidentally had an opportunity of visiting one of the training centres where his men are carrying on. At the present time in each training centre in Canada there is a personnel selection officer. He is one who has been trained in that sort of work, to give sample tests and also, by means of personal interviews with each man who is training in the training centre, to endeavour to establish the aptitude and capabilities of the men. Recommendations are made to the officer commanding the training centre with regard to the qualifications of a particular man. If they find a butcher, I think his presence will be advised to the quartermaster-general who has to do with the stores. If they find a blacksmith, his presence also will be advised to the quartermaster-general, and probably it will be notified as well to the commandant of the trade school at Hamilton where training in blacksmithing among fifty other trades is carried on. My hon. friend is quite right that many mistakes were made particularly when we were organizing the forces last year and the tremendous drive was on. We were building training centres and getting men there, getting staffs organized, and men were taken and trained in the particular subjects taught at that training centre. I have no doubt therefore that in many instances men were trained in one line even though their aptitude could have been put to better advantage somewhere else. I do not say that this has changed completely, but the system which has been in force is, if I may use the word, scientific; and I think it is a competent approach to this matter, which is extremely important and is becoming more so every day in connection with the armed services. The selection of mechanics particularly is vital to the armoured forces we have and to the mechanical trades which are needed in the infantry to-day. I have reason to believe that the personnel selection branch which has been organized for only a few months is doing most efficient work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
About how many men, skilled mechanics, have been taken out of the armed forces to go into munitions work?

speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that if I can avoid it, none are taken out of the armed forces to go into munitions work, because there is room in the armed forces for every mechanic. As I said, there are nearly fifty trades, thirty-five at least in the armoured division; mechanical men who are physically fit enlisting in the armed services can all be used to good advantage.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They told us at Aldershot that they did not have enough skilled men.

speechtext: Aldershot, Nova Scotia?

speechtext:
No,
England.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is the mechanical training school in Exhibition park at London, Ontario, under the minister's department?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is under my department. It is with the ordnance depot. I confess I have not been there. Our establishment is in new buildings there. Can my hon. friend tell me who is in charge? Is there an officer in charge?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I cannot say. There is one large building where there is an officer in charge; that is in the northeast corner of the city. But in the exhibition buildings there is a large mechanical school operated by the government. In my judgment that school is doing very fine work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That was our first
mechanization depot. We had a very large establishment there, put there primarily for the purpose of assembling and storing vehicles and having them ready to ship overseas as well as in Canada. Along with that the practical work provided gave opportunity to establish a school which has been operated for some time under the general staff and the master-general of ordnance. But whether the school to which my hon. friend refers is an army school I cannot tell. I have in mind that there is a commercial school as well.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There are two large depots, one of which does just what the minister says, assembles trucks and mechanical equipment from all round the country and repairs it and sends it forward. The day I was in the Exhibition park school there were perhaps one thousand young men learning all about cars, tanks and everything, and I was greatly struck with it. It is the only school I know of in the country where tlasses are taught by study of the actual
fMr. Castleden.]
machines and parts all cut open so that the classes can see just how they are put together. They told me they would be there for perhaps three or four months. I talked to many of the young men; they were all enthusiastic about how they were able to get along and learn. Apparently from there they are sent to different parts of the country. Why are there not more such schools, say one in the maritimes, and one in the western provinces? I believe the school is operated by a firm in the United States.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Anderson's.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I could see from my knowledge of mechanical equipment that they were doing a splendid job, and I would suggest that we should have such schools not only in London but one perhaps in Toronto, one in the maritimes and one in the west.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend has tied it down so that I know the school to which he refers is the school operated under the direction of the Department of National Defence. We got the Anderson company to come from the United States. They are also doing some instructing at Barriefield. It is called a mechanics' training school. That is an army school. In addition, we have a driving and maintenance school at Woodstock and the ordnance school at Barriefield, also a signal school at Barriefield and the Hamilton trade school at Hamilton.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But is any other school set up like the one in Exhibition park, London?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend knows the Hamilton trade school?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have visited the Hamilton trade school and I had an idea that the Anderson school at London was along the same lines.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I thought the London school was much more advanced.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
About a year ago we found the necessity for mechanics increasing all the time and felt that the quickest way to get them was to get people who had made a success of such schools in commercial work. The Anderson company had schools in California and elsewhere and they came and set up these schools. We have found it highly desirable to concentrate as much as possible, equipment being difficult to get. The air force found the same situation when

War Appropriation
they started their first initial training school. Therefore we have concentrated as much as possible in order to save both equipment and instructors. I think the plan is turning out very well. Of course my hon. friend understands that what we call phase 1 of the training is basic training. Then phase 2 is done all over the dominion in what were formerly the provincial technical schools, who do the elementary work in connection with mechanics. These are helped by the provinces. We have had fine cooperation from the provinces in that respect. Schools all over the dominion have been turned into trade schools for the benefit of the army. Then they go from there to either Hamilton or London or Barrie-field or Woodstock or some of these schools to take phases 3 and 4. My hon. friend says they stay for four months. Men in some trades stay longer; in the trade of fitter, which is needed badly, the course takes longer than four months. Generally speaking, I think an excellent job is being done in training tradesmen. Many of these men, unlike the one to whom my friend referred a moment ago, are men who had not had training at all; they are simply taken off the street and found to have an aptitude and put immediately into phase 2 and then phases 3 and 4.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Are these men given special rates of pay after graduation?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We have a tradesmen's establishment in connection with the various units. It may be a tank battalion or armoured battalion or any of these mechanized units, and the men in these establishments are given special trades pay.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: A few minutes ago in answer to the hon. member for Yorkton the minister said the equipment was examined and tested by the Department of National Defence-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The joint inspection board, representing the war office in England and the Department of National Defence in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Could the minister give some information about the results at the proving grounds in Canada? I am reluctant to ask any question tending to elicit information which the minister does not want to give, but at one time I heard some disconcerting reports, for instance about tanks made in Canada. The situation may have been improved since, or things may not be as I heard. Could the minister give any idea of the percentage of these tanks that had to be sent back from the proving grounds? Or if he is not prepared to give that, could he
say whether or not the percentage rejected has decreased to any extent? I should like some information with reference to other equipment as well, but particularly tanks.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I can say to the committee sincerely that I have not heard of any large or substantial number of tanks being rejected. Of course the very object of the proving ground is to find defects, and some of the tanks are tested to destruction intentionally; that is they are driven until they wear out or break. Both our tanks, since there are two models, have been sent to Aberdeen, Maryland, where there is an extensive proving ground, and we are now turning out tanks of both types in commercial quantities. I do not think many are being rejected now that they are in production. Of course my hon. friend understands that beginning with the transmission and on to the suspension, the engine, the turret and the track, all these are inspected separately before the tank is assembled, as well as the wireless equipment and the guns. Therefore, what you inspect in the complete tank is a combination or an assembly of things which already have been tried and tested. Perhaps my hon. friend could tell me privately anything he has heard about tanks being rejected in any quantity, because I think his information is incorrect, or he may have been hearing about the time when we were trying out models and ascertaining the best material or best type to use. I think we are now past the teething stage in connection with tanks, and the output has been gratifying having regard to all the difficulties we have had to meet.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am very glad indeed to hear that.
Some time ago the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar placed a question on the order paper and I believe it was passed as an order for return, which as yet has not come down. Could the minister give us any information with regard to insurance agents canvassing the soldiers for the purpose of selling life insurance policies and also what I believe are called savings bonds?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think I saw the answer to that question, and I thought it had been brought down some time ago. I believe there were two questions asked, the first being whether or not insurance agents were allowed to go to the camps. I believe the answer was that this depended on the district officer commanding, in connection with the regulations of the camp. Of course these agents would not be allowed in during parade hours or anything like that, but after hours it would depend on the district officer commanding and the
War Appropriation

particular regulations of the camp. To answer specifically, there were no general regulations prohibiting insurance agents going into camps. The second question was whether the government had examined the policies which were being sold, and that question I think was quite properly answered by saying it had been referred to the superintendent of insurance, because that is not a matter into which our department would examine.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It would seem that there might be some conference between the officials of the Department of National Defence and the superintendent of insurance, with a view to examining into that situation. The government should satisfy itself that the policies being sold to these men are pretty good financial propositions, and that these savings bonds and things of that sort are not merely rackets. It should know something about the amounts being paid. As a matter of fact, I was hoping for something along the line suggested by the hon. member for Peel this afternoon. If we are going to have any type of savings scheme at all-and I believe there should be some scheme-I had hoped that the government itself might institute it. If there is going to be any type of insurance policy for these men to pay on while they are on active service, the government itself should initiate it. Failing that, it seemed to me that the department would have some responsibility for a very close supervision of anything being sold to the men. After all most of these men have not had a great deal of experience in taking out insurance policies, or buying savings bonds, or anything of that sort, and I believe it is the responsibility of the government to see that any people allowed into the camps to sell commercial propositions like these adhere pretty strictly to some sort of regulation and submit to the government the proposition they are trying to sell. Otherwise I am afraid a great many of these boys, some of whom are handling money for the first time, may be victimized by salesmen.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Has my hon. friend any particular policy or any particular instance in mind?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No, no particular policy, but I have had letters from a large number of men and also from soldiers' wives, saying their husbands had taken out policies. The mere fact that they were so indefinite as to the benefits and provisions of the policies led me to believe these men had taken out policies without knowing very much about such things as maturity, cash surrender values and so forth. It seems to me they have been simply persuaded to take

out policies, for which they were paying so much money, with very little knowledge of the benefits they might receive.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The most important thing, of course, would be what would happen under such a policy in case the policyholder should become a war casualty. I would agree with my hon. friend that one should look out for matters of that kind in connection with these policies. Knowing the superintendent of insurance, I cannot imagine anybody selling a policy in the nature of a gold brick for very long in this country without being caught. I shall be glad, however, to have the officials confer with the insurance department, and also with one or two camp commandants, to see if policies are being sold and what is the nature of them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to add a further word in connection with the school in the Western exhibition grounds at London, Ontario. Since the school is filled with a great many machines which are fixed in place, is it the intention of the department to take over the exhibition grounds in London for the duration, as they have taken over the Canadian National Exhibition buildings in Toronto?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot make any statement in that regard at the moment. We have the buildings at present, but to be quite frank with my hon. friend I have not in mind at the moment the terms under which we now hold those buildings. I imagine they are leased for the duration, though I am not certain. I shall, however, ascertain the position, and if I can make any statement to my hon. friend with regard to future policy I shall be glad to do so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Personally I was sorry to read that the exhibition grounds in Toronto are not going to be used for exhibition purposes this fall. Perhaps they have been taken over at the request of the city; I do not know. Perhaps they have been taken over because the government needs the space which can be provided by the buildings, and I am sure, if that is the case, both the city and the exhibition authorities would be content to let the government have the buildings. But since reading that article I have been thinking: what about the great number of men and women who have been working in those exhibition grounds every year for perhaps the last twenty or thirty years? I have had a number of letters from people who have been in the habit of working there, wondering whether the government, in its agreement with the exhibition authorities

War Appropriation
to take over the buildings, is going to compensate those people who, after having worked ' there for perhaps fifteen or twenty years, now will lose their employment. Many of them have looked forward year after year to the extra money they make during the exhibition. That money is used for the payment of room rent, for the purchase of coal, and so forth. Has the department formulated any policy whatever to take care of people who are going to be unemployed as a result of the government taking over the grounds of the Canadian National Exhibition? The same remarks would, of course, apply if the government should take over the buildings of the Western exhibition at London.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is in the arrangement no provision to take care of those who may be unemployed by reason of the government taking over the exhibition grounds. I do not think there are going to be very many unemployed in the city of Toronto, though, of course, it may be that these are people who cannot work at other jobs. I am afraid, however, that in the exigencies of the war we shall have to ask them to make that contribution.
The taking over of the exhibition grounds was very carefully and seriously canvassed by defence council, by the chiefs of staff and by the deputy ministers of the departments concerned. I can say that it was not done at the request of the city or at the request of the province or at the request of the commission, though from all these sources we received the utmost cooperation that could be expected. A decision had to be arrived at after examining the alternative possibilities of moving out, as we have been doing in other years, or of building permanently a very large establishment somewhere else for all three services. As I said the other night, the navy have an establishment there, which is very well suited to their purposes, on the shore of the lake. They occupy that and expect to expand. The air force have a large establishment there as well, and moving would have meant interference with their activities. The army had not the same training situation as the other two services, but the army needed a depot, and needed it very badly. Having examined the cost of using the exhibition grounds for the duration of the war and paying a yearly amount therefor, implementing the arrangement which had been made between the city and the province, we felt that it was advantageous for the three services to stay there and that it was also in the national interest. An amicable arrangement was arrived at in very short order, having regard to the size of the proposal and the details which had to be worked out between
the city, the exhibition authorities and the province, and an order in council has been passed fully implementing the terms of the arrangement.

The minister a

speechtext:
I have mentioned the personnel selection branch. We put them to work at the very inauguration of the soldier's life at the basic training centres. To answer the hon. member's question specifically, the personnel selection men are on the move constantly on what we call a perpetual combing out of the units themselves, looking for men who have some special qualifications not needed in the particular unit. I would be obliged if my hon. friend would give me privately, if he does not mind, the names of, these men and their units, and I will do the rest. I found only last Saturday at a basic training centre a meteorologist in the ranks, but I also found that the personnel selection officer had already catalogued him and was sending his name in. I also found in the ranks two men who had had special jobs in the Department of National Defence at headquarters here. They had also been catalogued and their names sent in to the corps of military staff clerks.
The procedure at the basic training centre is for the personnel selection officer to interview each man. The selection officer calls for the roll of the men in the unit, and he goes through the ranks and ascertains the qualifications of the men.
My hon. friend asked, "are the officers of the units reluctant to let men with special skills go?" Having had to do with a unit myself, I know an officer is always reluctant to let such men go. He always thinks a radio expert, for example, might possibly go into a signal section before very long. At the same time, however, we have found cooperation. We have not found them intentionally hiding men with special skills, but they put up an argument to retain them for their own service, hoping they can be used in their own unit, and that is not unnatural.

speechtext:
There are two small matters I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. The first has to do with the travelling allowance for men on active service. I am not going to raise at this time the question of free transportation for soldiers; what I have in mind is the reduction in fare allowed to a man going on furlough. This reduction is granted only to his home, and it may well be that his wife and family have moved to another town, or that he wants, while on furlough, to visit his mother or other relatives. Many men have told me that they feel they should be allowed the cheaper rate while on furlough, even though they are not going home or to the place where they enlisted.
The other matter has to do with certain men who are giving a service but who may be termed the forgotten men. When the war started it was the apparent intention of the military authorities to have it a drab war; that is, there were to be no bands and no flying of flags. The war has been drab enough, but I do not think the situation has been improved by the lack of martial music. Of
late, a certain attempt has been made to supply military bands, but in certain towns the colonels of the regiments have formed bands, not entirely at their own expense but on their own volition. These bands are used when the men are on parade. In many instances the boys supply their own instruments and pay their own upkeep, and yet the bands are used on parade. It is unfortunate that we have not had more bands to lead out our men. Here in Ottawa you will see a small platoon walking through the streets without music or even a drum. We are all human, and I believe a certain amount of martial music should be provided for platoons or regiments.
As I say, these men are giving their time as bandsmen; they are not receiving one penny more than the ordinary soldier, and I contend that they should be classified properly and given a little encouragement. They are serving a useful purpose. I was invited to meet some of these boys and found that they are supplying their own instruments and putting in their practice, and yet the military authorities will not designate them either as tradesmen or bandsmen. It is high time that some encouragement was given to these boys who are rendering such a splendid service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend is right when he says that at the beginning of the war there were few bands authorized, but I think I am correct in saying that we have authorized a band for every active unit that has requested one. Not only have we authorized that the instruments be supplied, but we have authorized the personnel, to a limited number, of course.
I shall deal now with the question of trades pay. This matter has been up before. I am not quite as much impressed as my hon. friend is with the matter of trades pay for bandsmen. I know these men are rendering a splendid service. I happen to have had two bands in my own battalion, but they were men who were on the strength in the regular way and were giving their time. My hon. friend will be glad to know there was a pipe band as well as a brass band.
As I say, the matter of trades pay for bandsmen has been up, and up repeatedly. It is not settled yet as far as that goes. But I must say that I do not see the argument for trades pay for bandsmen as clearly as my hon. friend does. It seems to me that if men are taken on the establishment as bandsmen and love music as my hon. friend does, they will not insist upon trades pay in order to enjoy the privilege of playing. We have authorized a band for each advanced
War Appropriation

training centre; that is the establishment and the instruments. This is done on the authorization of the minister, and I may say that I have approved every application which has been made. We authorize the instruments for the basic training centres, but we do not authorize the men. They must be men from the establishment, but we make a small allowance of $200 a year. I want to assure my hon. friend that the matter of bands is not being overlooked. I think the real objection he has to our present system is the fact that so far bandsmen have not been recognized as tradesmen, but this matter has been under consideration for some time.
