subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There are one or two
matters about which I should like to ask the minister. The first has to do with the dependents' allowance, as amended last November. There is a great difference of opinion as to how this is working out. May 1 is housing day, and a great many soldier families in military district No. 2 have been ordered out of their homes. They receive very little protection from the federal law. This is not the fault of the minister; I am free to admit that all parties in the house are to blame for our lack of defences because of their support of pacifism for years before the war and the league. It was not to be expected that you could rearm or do this in a year or two years or three years when you threw away your defences like you did. A high cost of living bonus is needed very badly by the soldiers' wives and families. They have been urged to get in their coal for next winter, and there is a great scarcity of houses in the city from which I come.
I urge the government to reconsider the proposal to give a high cost of living bonus to the soldier and grant it to them. I fail to see why all civilians who stay at home should be the only people to get the bonus, while those who are defending us for $1.30 a day in England are denied it. All should receive it equitably. Both classes need it.
The minister has made a great many improvements; I am free to admit that he did well over a year ago in appointing Colonel MacNamara, who has done splendid work while there in remedying inequalities and getting the pay cheques direct to the dependents.

On September 9, 1939, the house was given a schedule of pay for the army, the navy and the air force. The house was not consulted; it was a hard and fast schedule attached to the Canadian Patriotic Fund Act, and passed in about half an hour. The minister has been kind enough to promise to provide us with a list of the pay of officers and all ranks from a colonel down. The inequalities are apparent to anybody who looks it over. The inequalities are unjust and unfair. We shall soon be in the position of Kentucky and Missouri, where everybody wants to be a colonel or a judge; down there every lawyer is called judge, because if he is not judge to-day he hopes to be a judge to-morrow. So with our army. I repeat that the inequalities in the schedule of the three forces are very apparent. I trust that the house will give more attention to this particular matter, and seek a new and fairer schedule.
The vote yesterday shows that Canadians are greatly alarmed at the state of this country's defences. Germany has now entered her third spring offensive. What are we in Canada doing to meet the enemy, whether he comes to the front door, the side door or the back door-and dear knows he is at all the doors now. I contend that we should heed the handwriting on the wall. It may be necessary to change our whole method of training and strategy in the twinkling of an eye, in view of our allies' disasters. I know the minister has seen the report of Lieutenant-General Gordon Bennett made to the British government as to what was wrong with the Pacific campaign on land, on sea, and in the air. I wish that every hon. member could be given a copy of that report and would carefully study it. Remember that the training, the strategy and the equipment which we are now following may be obsolete and as worthless as a scrap of paper in twenty-four hours. The whole war and its conduct is a ceaseless change every year. A great deal of our present discussion for that reason may not be relevant later. There is need for effective coordination between the services.
As I interpret the vote of the people yesterday, it is a demand for not less but more real war effort, so that our sacrifices, which have been many, may not have been in vain; so that we shall make better use of the splendid men in our armed forces, see that they are properly armed, and give them a real show in battle. I admit that a great deal has been done; in many departments the war effort has been effective. But I press upon the attention of hon. members the report which was made to the British and Australian governments on the disasters in

War Appropriation
Malaya and generally in the Pacific so that we may not fall into similar traps. The report was transmitted to Australia, and as a result a serious effort at coordination has been made there. After yesterday we can get rid of our cobwebs, prejudices and inertia, come down from the clouds, and have a total war effort with clarity, energy, wisdom and strength of thought and action. We need more clarity and energy and more fearlessness of thought. The vote yesterday exhibits the anxiety of the average voter as to the outcome of this titanic world struggle; the demand is for a greater and better effort in view of the money we are spending-four million dollars a day.
What are our objectives for 1942 and planning and strategy in the light of the changes which have been brought about in the scope and strategy of the war by Germany and Japan and their directors of training? Our plans should be formulated and acted upon now before it is too late. This is the third spring of the German offensive. The first spring she captured the whole of western Europe. The second spring offensive began in the conquest of the Balkans and continued until the conquest of Greece. The third offensive may come to Canada. Nobody can tell. It is speculative, at present. It is generally supposed to be directed towards the Caucasus, but that may not be the only offensive. Hitler is the grand master of timing. So I say we should revise our schedule and syllabus, and revise our programme in view of this and other expected emergencies. The enemy is about to try a new effort and plan on the Atlantic. Hitler will probably invade Portugal; he may take Spain; and if he cuts our life lines of communications on the Atlantic with the United States, I do not know where the allies are going to be. We face now tremendous odds at sea and on the land. We may be assailed by Hitler from the direction of an attempt to take Iceland. Our fine friends of the United States have done a great deal well, but, as was shown in the Pacific, they are not ready for war and her rearming is far behind schedule to Russia and Britain. Japan destroyed the best part of their navy and they are confronted with serious strategic problems. It is not the will but the power that is wanting. In addition to that, they are not ready as a military power, and we cannot expect them to be ready, because they were an unmilitary power, untrained and unprepared, much in the position of Great Britain after Dunkirk. When they are ready, in a year the war will change at once. It will take them nearly two years to get completely ready, and Hitler is well
aware of the fact and wants a knockout in 1942. We should amend our programme to fit in with the realities of the third German spring offensive. Until Britain and the United States have regained control of the Pacific, Canada is in a very dangerous position. So are India, Australia, Ceylon, Burma, Madagascar and South Africa.
I sympathize with the minister in occupying the position he does at the present time.
I do not believe that he ever was a pacifist, but this house was imbued solidly with pacifism and disarmament, with the result that it is going to take us a long time to get us into the position in which we should be. Britain, France, and other democracies have suffered the consequences of the same attitude of mind, because they threw away their defences and friends.
I suggest that the minister is fully aware of the fact that we are opposed by a first-class naval and air power in the Pacific. For the first time in nearly 100 years Great Britain has been driven out of southern Asia and India. Japan, no doubt, has other designs and will engage in new attacks. Already she threatens Ceylon and India; she has overrun Burma, and there are reports of an attack on Madagascar, which would bring her to the front door of South Africa and her eastern shores in the Indian ocean. The threat to South Africa is a very real one, and all classes, including the natives, are being mobilized. She has had a bad scare, as has our whole empire.
In the Pacific, three dominions-South Africa, New Zealand and Australia-are near the danger zone. They are looking for aid to the United States, and while the United States is sending men of a good type, we know that men who are not fully trained are of little use to-day and are not ready. Here let me refer to a report which was made by Doctor van Mook, the great Dutch governor general and patriot of Java. Recently he flew to Australia, and he has given Australians some good advice. He does not say anything inimical to Britain, which had promised Java some help that failed to come; he has shown himself a great patriot; and his report is of real significance to Canada, because it proves that without an adequate armed force neither this nor any other dominion in our empire can continue to exist. Only one thing matters in our empire-the military power to defend it.
The very fate of the British empire is now at stake. It is threatened not only in South Africa, Australia and New Zealand but here as well. Let me give you the splendid advice which the great patriot
War Appropriation

soldier I named of the Dutch Netherlands gave to Australia-and Canada also should hearken to these recommendations. In the first place, he said, the war should be waged by air and sea. In the second place, the Japanese supply lines are vulnerable; and third, Japan has so many soldiers that even if a large number are killed it will not make much difference. They have, however, strained their resources and now are trying to link up with the Italian and German front in order to get a foothold in north and west Australia and with Italy and Germany. He recommends some simple truths as a means of avoiding the setting up of separate commands. Remember, he says, that this is a totalitarian war. Put aside politics and those aspects of it which do not directly bear upon the war. Do not use untrained men. Whenever the Dutch had anything like equal chance in Java against Japan in the air they dealt with them successfully, he says; but when we were outnumbered ten to one the merits of the pilot hardly entered into the calculation. That is excellent advice which that great man has given on military and political strategy to all our empire.
We are spending money on munitions and equipment that may be obsolete to-morrow. It has been shown since this war started that the methods which have been adopted have been inadequate to cope with Japan and Germany. Germany with her mechanized horde simply marched through Europe. It has been shown that at Singapore they were overmechanized. General Bennett has described the Jap tactics and the chief weapons they used. What we may be looking for if they invade Canada may not be the weapons that they will use. What were the weapons which they have already used? The machine gun, the tommy gun, the rifle and the bayonet. Their maim tactics consisted in infiltration by small, daringly led patrols who were sometimes mounted on captured cycles and who pushed far ahead of the regular troops. The House of Commons in London was told on March 27 that Singapore fell because munitions had to be given to Russia and Libya. That is wrong according to the Bennett report. This authority declares that it was the lack of sufficiently numerous and adequately trained and equipped and well commanded forces of infantry to counter the Japanese infiltration tactics that was responsible for the reverses, even though at Singapore their armoured force and their air force and artillery were outnumbered. These are only a few of the

matters which are dealt with in the Bennett report and by the commanding officer of Dutch Java.
I admit that the government is faced with a very trying and difficult task to rearm, especially the minister who has to bear the brunt of these three services, because I think he is bearing the brunt of the whole thing. I should like to see better attention paid to soldiers and their dependents. I should like to see a reallotment of pav and reconsideration by the military experts of the report of General Bennett, and other reports which have been submitted to the British government and which have stirred up criticism in conflict with the non-military experts. Japan got back to simple methods and more of the 1918 mentality of warfare- as I say, the infiltration tactics by the surprise of infantry. That was not a new venture in this war. It was adopted by the Germans in 1918 against Britain and France when they made raids without tanks, and it was successful. They captured a lot of equipment and prisoners, as did the allies also in similar tactics later.
Simplicity has been vindicated not only on land and sea but in the air on the Pacific and in other theatres of war. There is bound to be criticism; but criticism is a tonic, or to change the metaphor, it is a weapon that strengthens the hands of the minister. The government must expect reasonable criticism, and I may say that the_ criticism here cannot compare with the criticism that takes place in Australia and the United States. I hope that now a further contribution will be made to the dependents of soldiers and that there will be better equipment. The minister has said that he has been giving attention to this, and I believe he has been giving attention to it in the last twelve months.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There are a few matters which I wish to call to the attention of the committee with a view to securing from the minister certain information, which up to the present time the committee has not received. The vote on the plebiscite yesterday brought under immediate consideration the question of the mobilization of the man-power of this nation. On April 23, the minister, in answer to a question asked by myself as reported at page 1904 of Hansard used these words:
I thiqk I intimated when I spoke in February that my advice was that if enlistments were maintained within a reasonable distance, I think I said, of that level, we would be able to take care of our commitments.

War Appropriation
That answer was given to a question which I asked and which read:
Should the voluntary enlistments continue at the rate prevailing since January, would there be sufficient to meet the present needs of the army and the anticipated needs during the present year?
I think now, in view of the tremendous and overwhelmingly favourable vote yesterday and the decisions which will have to be taken in connection with further mobilization of our man-power, the committee should be made cognizant of the facts relating to the mobilization of our men up to the present time. The minister stated that during the months of January, February and March some 29,000 men voluntarily joined the active service forces of Canada, and he gave details of the numbers who had enlisted month by month.
I asked a question, the information with respect to which was not then before him, and I think it is necessary that this committee should be possessed of this information if it is to be in a position to have a proper perspective of the man-power situation. How many men were discharged during the same period?
Another question which I asked and on which the committee should have information is this. When the minister points out that some 29,000 men have enlisted in the army during the last three months, before we are in a position to know whether these were voluntary enlistments or not, we should be furnished with information as to how many of them were of the age limits 18 and 19 and then again from 20 to 24. When I asked the minister for this information the other day he said he was unable to give it at the moment. I hope he has the information now, because by no manner of means can many of those who enlisted in the active army be called voluntary enlistments,, having regard to the system which is now general over all this dominion so far as young men are being compulsorily called and who enlist in the active army thereafter are concerned. There is not a day passes that hon. members do not receive letters to the effect that after these men are called up they are subjected to all kinds of intimidation with a view to securing their enlistment for overseas service. They are badgered, bulldozed and browbeaten. Therefore, to be in a position to judge whether or not these are voluntary enlistments and the voluntary system can continue in the months to come to supply the necessary numbers, we must be informed of the ages of those who are enlisting.

People ask why men do not join the army, and in what I have to say now I refer particularly to those who live in areas in which there are congregated large bodies of conscientious objectors. I am not one of those who suggest that because a man conscientiously believes it is wrong to participate in war, every regard and consideration should not be given that man's religious feelings. That is right and proper, but here is the objection which I have heard stated so frequently by men living in those districts, who have sons and brothers overseas. The services of conscientious objectors consist in going to a national park for a period of four months, during which *time they are paid. After they have worked there for that length of time, their service to their country, for the entire period of the war, is over. Is there any justification for that? I suggest to the minister that while we should respect rigidly the beliefs of those who conscientiously object to war service, every man in this country within the age limit set out in the mobilization act should be required to serve for the same length of time, and that the contribution of these people in the period of service should be the same as that of the men who are subject to call for service in the army.
What I have stated, Mr. Chairman, in general summarizes the suggestions I have to offer, except for one further point which I raised last fall and which I raise again this evening. I have in my files a letter from a man who served overseas in the last war. He was blinded in the service of his country and receives a pension of $75 a month. On January 1, 1942, he received notification from the Department of Finance that in consequence of a ruling made by a department of government, his pension would be subject to the national defence tax. That was not a ruling of parliament. That ruling was not the consequence of a statute passed by parliament. It was made under a ruling of an administrative body, and not under an act of parliament. When I brought up this question the last time the Minister of National Defence for Air indicated that he would give consideration to the situation, with a view to ascertaining whether or not such a regulation was legally in effect and, if so, whether consideration might be given to the introduction of the legislation necessary to relieve these 100 per
cent pensioners from the payment of such tax. I think we all agree that the men in the army should receive the utmost consideration. I was glad to hear the minister say the other evening, if I understood him correctly, that the discrimination which heretofore existed in favour of the air force as against the army, in the matter of transportation, had been removed. It should be removed. On more than one trip from western Canada I had occasion to see men who were being sent from one part of Canada to the other, under conditions which were anything but favourable to enlistment by those who might see those men in those circumstances.
These may be said to be little things. But, Mr. Chairman, it is these little things which, when rectified, will result in a great improvement in the morale of our troops. All of us in this parliament want to do our part. It is not as a demagogue that I speak; that is not at all the spirit in which I have addressed these remarks to the committee. Throughout this day the arguments that have been advanced in regard to the problems of the soldier have come from this side of the house. That is not because hon. members in other parts of the house do not agree with a great deal of what has been said, but I do think that regardless of what side of the house we are on, it is our duty at this time to bring to the attention of hon. members and of the government such matters as we believe will improve the position of any service men and their dependents and will ensure that they will receive the consideration which can be accorded to them.

This is the most important item of the estimates. Before the Easter adjournment $500,000,000 was voted, and the measure now before the committee provides for the expenditure of a further billion and a half. Our duty here is to check the expenditures, according to the old British principle of ministerial responsibility for the expenditure of public money. The responsibility is all the greater by reason of the fact that we have no detailed estimates for such tremendous amounts of money.
It has been the custom for several years for members of parliament to lay their grievances before the minister, as though they were laying them at the foot of the throne.
Of course, the function of the cabinet is
War Appropriation

entirely different from that of the throne, and if the throne has the right of grace, which the cabinet does not have, the cabinet has the duty to render an account of all expenditures, even down to the cents, which the throne has not. In order that there shall be no confusion, I establish that distinction before expressing my views on the discussion of estimates in this committee of the House of Commons.
What member knows the organization of the Department of National Defence as it now stands? Of course, there are charts made by draftsmen, showing the organization of each department. Those charts are not available to members. But, since necessity is the mother of invention, I have found a sketch of the department in the dominion government telephone directory. That is just a commonplace book which appears on the desk of every member of the house and of every official who has the right to a telephone number of his own. In this directory under National Defence Department (Army) there commences a list, under subtitles of the different branches of the department, starting at page 80 and going on for several pages. I see a mass of paper on the desk in front of the minister at the moment. There are several brief cases and a big box which must be full of information. That information we want, and we have a right to get it. When we are here in the committee of this House of Commons to discuss estimates, we are not here to put the minister through the third degree. We are here to know what is done with the public moneys which come from the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada. We want to know what use has been made of that money. If the use is good, the department is praised and so is the minister. If the use is bad, then the department and the minister have to be blamed. That is only common sense, and it is in accordance with the old tradition of British parliamentary practice, as is known to every hon. member of the house, even if it is ignored by a large number of dominion government officials.

The hon. member for Lake Centre referred to the matter of discharges. He asked how many had been discharged during the three months period January to March. The exact number is 4,482, in England and in Canada. That is something like half of one
War Appropriation

per cent per month, which I think is quite a normal figure of wastage. The number discharged as physically unfit, included in that figure, is 3,261.
The hon. member asked how many had enlisted between the ages of eighteen and nineteen. As I advised him, I have not the figures, and the only way of getting them that I know of would be to go through the attestation papers individually. But it developed that the real reason why my hon. friend wanted this information was to be able to demonstrate that the enlistments, the record of which I had given for January, February and March, 28,686, had come from men who, to use his own expression, had been bludgeoned and browbeaten in the miltiary training centres and that he wanted to show that they came within that age limit. 1 can tell him that he does not need that information in order to find out pretty accurately how many were men from the training centres. Of the number who enlisted in that time approximately 16 per cent were men from the training centres. That means something like 4.000 out of the 28,000 enlisted from training centres or National Resources Mobilization Act camps. Therefore I do not think my hon. friend should feel that those enlistments are very seriously boosted or increased by men from training centres. The figures for April are now practically complete, because we are close to the end of the month. Over 10,000 enlisted, so that the figures for the first four months are something like 38,000 or 39,000 altogether, and of those, on the same percentage, something like 5,800 would have enlisted from the training centres.
I want to repudiate in the strongest possible terms the statement that men are bludgeoned, browbeaten and generally forced to join the army. I have stated to the committee on previous occasions that when reports have come to me from time to time or statements been made such as my hon. friend made to-night, I have investigated them and have found no grounds for any statement that there was undue or improper pressure except on one occasion, and I took prompt action in connection with that. I say to the committee that the recruiting figures are not built up to any extent by recruiting from the training centres. I do not think my hon. friend does recruiting good service when he makes statements of that kind. There is no doubt that in the training centres the men themselves, men who are "active" as they call it, bring a certain amount of pressure to bear, but I have also indicated that I have been in a number of evangelistic meetings in my youth in which exactly the same sort of enthusiasm

and pressure was used. I have said and I repeat that the instructions are that there shall be no difference whatever in treatment in the training centres. Leave is given to men who enlist to allow them to go home and arrange their affairs, but as far as treatment is concerned they are given exactly the same treatment as the others. The orders are that there is to be no discrimination of any kind, no undue pressure, no improper influence used. If any hon. members have any cases to bring to my attention, I will see that they are investigated as thoroughly as possible.
My hon. friend dealt with the matter of pay and allowances. That had a pretty thorough discussion this afternoon. I do not think there is anything I can add to what I have said.
The cost of living bonus was discussed to-night by the hon. member for Broadview. I did not reply to him because I had already said what I had to say on that.
My hon. friend referred to pay and allowances in the United States. He knows they are considerably below Canadian rates. Those below7 the rank of warrant officers get no dependents' allowance at all, whereas since the beginning of the war we have been paying them and paying rates higher than those in the United States. There is a movement going on now to increase the rates of pay there.
I have said I will give consideration to the representations made respecting dependents' allowances and the suggestion as to deferred pay.
My hon. friend made another suggestion, namely, in regard to Indians. I do not know whether he was in the committee this afternoon when I dealt with the matter of dependents' allowances to those who are in the West Indies. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar brought it up. When I went to investigate the question of dependents' allowances to those in the West Indies, Jamaica particularly, I found that a reduction had been made to some of the Indians in this country. Exactly the same action will be taken and, as a matter of fact, has been taken in connection with the Indians as I indicated would be taken with regard to those in the West Indies. That is to say, the amount of 835 for the wife's allowance will be paid in full, and will not be subject to any reduction. I may add that in connection with Indians there are some cases, as my hon. friend may understand-and this does not apply to Indians alone but also to other citizens of Canada-where it is thought well, both under the Pension Act and under the

With regard to conscientious objectors, I think I caught the drift of what my hon. friend said. He was indicating, I understood, that they should serve in some non-combatant *capacity, for the same length of time as those who are called up to serve in the armed forces. There is no reason in the world, as far as legal power is concerned, why this should not be done, and I shall bring it to the attention of my colleagues who have been dealing with this question, one of whom has just come into the house.
This matter has been brought to my attention in another way. The suggestion has been made that there is a place in the armed forces where these conscientious objectors could serve; that is to say, in the medical corps. I have taken the position, rightly or wrongly, that the men who serve in the armed forces must be in a position to take on whatever is necessary in the army. I do not want a distinction made between the duties which *men may be called upon to perform. As a matter of fact, from time to time we may have medical orderlies who go into other branches, or who come from other services. Someone

may come from headquarters into the medical corps, or on the other hand a medical orderly may go to headquarters duty. I have a distinct recollection of a time when medical orderlies, cooks, batmen and everyone else went into the line. To make any distinction of the kind in a unit I do not think is for the good of the unit itself, so I would hesitate to have men in the unit who could not be called upon to do combatant service.

The men in the army do not profess to be infallible; but they cannot speak for themselves, and I say to my hon. friend that I do not propose to have a statement of that sort go unchallenged. I have received and this country has received loyal support and loyal and efficient service from the men in the army; and I want to say to my hon. friend! that I think it ill becomes a member of parliament to stand in his place here and make a statement of that kind.
In connection with the salaries which are paid to men in the army, I may say to the hon. member that as a matter of fact most of those men are not professional soldiers at all. They are men who have been in the militia. Most of them served in the last war. They have been called in and have changed their profession for the time being in order to help out .in connection with war work. There are a certain number of professional soldiers, and thank heaven there are, because we did not treat our pro-
fessional soldiers any too well, at least during the period when I was Minister of National Defence previously. I take my share of responsibility for that. From 1926 to 1930 the army and national defence services were nearly starved, and I make that statement now. It seemed to me that perhaps the most popular indoor sport in those days was cutting amounts off the estimates for national defence, and the hon. member for Temiscouata did his share of advocating that this be done. Now I say to my hon. friend that in spite of all that, the men who were professional soldiers did keep on. The organization that we have to-day, which does not suit my hon. friend, does not suit me nor does it suit the men who are in it, but it is an organization that had to be built from the ground up. I say that when you expand an organization from ten thousand men, as it existed on September 9, 1939, to about three hundred thousand men as it exists to-day in the army alone; when over 425,000 men have been enlisted; when you have had the expansion which the establishments of the army have had from the Atlantic to the Pacific, not only in connection with operations but in connection with training; when you have sent overseas the men who have been sent and the organizations which are over there, it has meant a tremendous amount of work. I was glad my hon. friend read the list which he did read, because it indicated the multiplicity of activities which are carried on by the Department of National Defence. We have to enlist and train and clothe and house and feed these men. We have to move them from place to place. We have to see that they are supplied with proper rations; we have to see that they are furnished with training facilities, that armaments are supplied, that arrangements are made for getting them across the country and over on the other side of the ocean, and then we have to arrange for the same things over there. Therefore the activities carried on by the department are not small, and I make no apology for the list which my hon. friend has read or the list which he could have put on record.
I say to my hon. friend now that if he will look at the tabulation which I put on the record this afternoon, he will see the salaries for the men in the army from the rank of colonel down, and I give now the information I was asked for this afternoon, a statement with regard to the salaries in the army from the rank of colonel up, so that my hon. friend and other hon. gentlemen will know exactly what salaries are being paid.

War Appropriation
The highest pay in the army is that of the Army Commander, General A. G. L. McNaughton-a total of $14,000 per annum, without any additional allowances.
The two corps commanders are each paid $10,585 per annum, with dependents' allowances in addition.
Divisional commanders are paid $8,760 per annum, with the same allowances.
District officers commanding are graded in class 3 with pay of $6,205 per annum, plus the same allowances. Where they are compelled to provide their own quarters and subsistence, an allowance of $365 per annum is added.
Other officers of the rank of brigadier and up usually hold staff appointments in which they are graded according to classification. The higher classifications are listed in article 124 of Financial Regulations and Instructions. The chief of the general staff is paid by order in council a flat amount of $10,000 without any allowance; the adjutant-general and the quartermaster-general are paid $7,300 per annum. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is a difference
between better and best. His best speech was when he complained of the brass hats in the Department of National Defence, and when he spoke on that I cheered him heartily and banged my desk and said to myself, here is one man who is not afraid to tell the truth.
I say that in the army there are not only good men but very good men. But the value of an officer is not in his uniform alone or in the shine of his boots. It is in his brains and in the kindness of his heart. The minister was right when he said the other day that every commanding officer should be like a father to those in his regiment under him. But what I find is that the soldiers are very often exchanging their fathers, meaning by that, that recruits and soldiers of my county are presently defending British Columbia. I do not complain about that. I understand that this is their country and our country from ocean to ocean. But what was extraordinary was this. I was informed by the Department of National Defence, dated April 6, telling me that a farmer's son had been given six months' leave to return to cultivate his father's land. I was greatly surprised two weeks later to receive a letter from this young man, who was at first at Valcartier, Quebec. It had been posted under date of April 20, at Nanaimo, British Columbia. This young man was awarded six months' leave by the constituted authority, the commission of national war services, but he could not enjoy that leave because the Department of National Defence did not stand by the decision of the commission which, according to the national war regulations, is final. The Department of National Defence did not respect the law; they took that boy and instead of sending him to his father to cultivate the farm, they sent him to British Columbia. He was never informed that he had been given that leave. I do not know if that was done in bad faith or through ignorance, but it was done just the same. Here we have an example of disrespect of constituted authority, disrespect exemplified by that action of the Department of National Defence.
The minister said, in the first place, that I spoke too long and, in the second place, that he was glad that I read part of the long list of departments under his control. He said it is costly because there are so many. I do not object to the minister having a number of branches in his department provided they are useful and provided that these people do not spend their time clicking their heels and spurs on Sparks street, Slater street, Elgin street and the other streets in Ottawa, showing how important they are. What they should do is not to show that they are important-I say this to the minister as well as to his subalterns [DOT]-they should show that they are useful, that they are defending this country well and are making the best possible use of the men who are serving in the three branches.
When we dare to raise our voices to complain of injustices we receive the spurn of contempt, we hear contemptuous laughing; we do not need that. I will tell the minister once again what the greatest soldier of our times, Marshal Foch, said about the military art. He said that it was based on common sense, meaning that every action of the army had to be justified on the basis of common sense. Common sense is accessible to all; it is not an unusual gift. If the minister acts in fairness to all, to the army as well as to the members of the House of Commons; if he wants to act in fairness to all, he should go on in the way of his first steps to-night. He should give us more information, not only about the salaries paid in the Department of National Defence, but also about the expenditures for travelling, for allowances and other things.
We want a policy of national defence that can be commended to the Canadian people, that will satisfy the Canadian people and that will mostly satisfy Canadian soldiers, Canadian sailors and Canadian airmen. The minister may be a great man. I am a humble private member of this hon. house, but I am ready to do anything to help the Department of National Defence provided we get rid of all the nonentities who are there and who are responsible for the things like the one I have
